# Study of the Causes of Boom Elements Cracking of Electric Demolition Machine with Use of Experimental and Numerical Methods

Damian Derlukiewicz1  and Maciej Cieślak2

(1)

Department of Machine Design and Research, Wrocław University of Science and Technology, Lukasiewicza 7/9, 50371 Wroclaw, Poland

(2)

Centre for Mobility and Transport, Coventry University, Priory Street, Coventry, CV1 5FB, UK

Damian Derlukiewicz (Corresponding author)

Email: damian.derlukiewicz@pwr.edu.pl

Maciej Cieślak

Email: cieslakm@coventry.ac.uk

Abstract

In this study authors present a method which was used to investigate the causes of boom elements cracking on Brokk90 demolition machine. This type of machine is used by ARCAD demolition company from Wrocław, Poland. Their specialty are demolition jobs, which require use of wide variety of equipment. In particular they offer demolition with use of small remotely controlled robots. In this case operators of the Brokk90 machine discovered crack growth which appeared on the sections of the arm system, to which a variety of tools can be mounted such as hydraulic breakers, hydraulic cutters, diamond chain saws etc. Crack growth occurred much earlier than time before overhaul designed by the manufacturer. The investigation of the of the arm system was carried out by the authors of this paper. In order to minimize the time during which the machine will not be operational, it has been decided to use noninvasive methods of measuring and recording the movement of the arm system during operation. Techniques used for this study consists of using Phantom high speed camera and Commtest vb7 vibrometer. Clips recorded via the high speed imagining system were processed using state of the art processing software which determined excitation acting on the arm system while in operation. Use of vibrometer allowed to investigate natural frequencies of the assembly, and later on validate built FEA model. Based on recorded data boundary conditions for the simulations were determined and used in the simulation. During the study a fully functional finite element analysis model of the arm system was developed. Study of the model allowed researchers to thoroughly investigate stresses occurring in the elements of the arm sections. Based on the similarity between places of stress concentration on the model and places of crack formation on the arm system, high level of correlation between real life machine and simulation model was established.

## 1 Introduction

Demolition machines are widely used on modern construction sites. It would not be possible to demolish, redesign or build new buildings as quickly as it is nowadays without them. Almost all companies use hydraulic breakers due to their robustness and precision. Within the market for heavy duty demolition machines there has been a niche for small demolition vehicle solution which has been taken over by couple companies amongst which the two major ones are Brokk and Husqvarna. Both those companies offer similar solutions. The interest for those machines is constantly growing due to their size, mobility, ability to work nonstop, multiple shifts and possibility to decrease dangers to the operator. One of the companies using Brokk machines is ARCAD, which is based in Wroclaw, Poland. This company specializes in demolitions jobs and specifically uses demolition robots for various type of demolition work. Goal of the company is maximize profitability with simultaneous decrease of the costs. Operators and maintenance staff from ARCAD realized that Brokk90 machines in the company require more time servicing due to appearance of crack on the sections of the boom system. The company turned to the researchers from Wroclaw University of Technology who were asked to investigate the problem and propose a solution. During the initial investigation assumption was made that increase wear of the arm system might be caused by vibrational nature of the conditions under which it is operating. ARCAD has set a goal to identify the source of crack growth and propose and alteration to the design or proposition of a reinforcement of the existing arm system solution. This particular research is part of a bigger project which goal is design of new arm system solution based on the methodology developed during investigation of current Brokk 90 arm system. In this paper researchers used noninvasive methods such as high speed imaging and vibrometer measurements along with finite element analysis simulations to determine the source of the problem.

## 2 Small Demolition Machines—Brokk 90

Currently on the market of small, remotely controlled demolition equipment there are couple of companies which provide such solutions to the end customers. Majority of the market has been taken over by Brokk and Husqvarna, which are both based in Sweden. However it has to be noted that there are other companies which do not necessarily focus only on small demolition robots but offer them to widen their lineup of demolition tools. Those companies are FERRI from Italy or Avant from Finland. Last group of manufacturers are the ones from emerging markets such as Giant from China or JP-ROK from India.

Brokk 90 is a small demolition machine which is controlled using a wired or wireless controller (Fig. 1). This type of demolition vehicle is one of the smallest available on the market. With attached but retracted arm system the dimensions of the machine itself are 1380 mm in height and only 780 mm wide. Brokk90 with necessary fluids such as hydraulic oil weighs 1065 kg.

Fig. 1

Brokk 90 demolition machine with SB152 hydraulic breaker attached [1, 2]

The design which is characterized by small dimensions and relatively small mass allow the machine to operate inside of the building and in narrow corridor. Low placement of the center of gravity of the assembled machine allows it to climb steep hills or drive inside the staircases. Use of rubber tracks distributes the mass of the machine along large surface area underneath it. The machine can be divided into three main subassemblies. The first one is the driving unit which consists of electric and hydraulic motors, oil tank and the tracks. Brokk90 machine hydraulic system consists of gear pump connected to the electric ABB M2AA motor. The second subassembly is the arm system or the boom. This subsystem consists of three section foldable boom. Three sections are connected with revolute joints. Entire arm system is driven by set of three hydraulic pistons which are powered by hydraulic pump. The base of the arm system is attached to the driving unit via a turntable which allows it for a rotation within 245º around vertical axis of the machine. Time required for a full rotation from end to end is only 8 s. The last subassembly which can be defined within small demolition machine is the tool connected to the boom system. The manufacturer provides the end user with a variety of hydraulically powered tools. One of the most used solutions are the hydraulic breaker which has been specifically designed for that vehicle and hydraulic cutters.

Due to the fact that the machine is powered by a three phase 380 V electric motor it has an ability to operate is small confined spaces with very limited ventilation. The robot is controlled by an operator via a wireless remote which allows him to conduct demolition work from a distance of up to 100 m. By removing the operator from the proximity of the machine increase in operator safety is provided. It also benefits the user of the machine because it does not expose the operator to various types of vibrations and noise which are generated by the hydraulic breaker. This allows the operator to work in a safer, quitter and more comfortable environment.

During the operation of the machine the operators in ARCAD company noticed crack showing in various places of the boom system (Fig. 2). During regular maintenance the cracks have been removed by welding the sections of the boom together. However, this solution was not permanent. ARCAD turned to the researchers from Wroclaw University of Technology to investigate the source causing the cracks to appear.

Fig. 2

Cracks on the second section of the arm system used on Brokk 90 machine

## 3 Field Measurements of the Brokk 90

Due to the fact that ARCADs goal was to minimize downtime in machine operation during field testing and data collection authors of this paper decided to use noninvasive methods. Even though it would be more convenient to move the Brokk to a closed facility and create perfect data collection conditions. In this case it was not an option so researchers decided to use two techniques which are relatively quick to apply and provide good level of accuracy. The measurement techniques used for collection of data were high speed imaging (Fig. 3) and measurements with vibrometer Commtest vb7.

Fig. 3

Brokk 90 and high speed camera setup

Recording from high speed camera was used to set up the boundary conditions for the simulation model. Camera used for the recording, the Phantom V12 is capable of recording up to 1 million frames per second (FPS). For purposes of this experiment black and white recording at 720 pixels in height was recorded. Maximum frame rate for this resolution in that case is equal to 6224 FPS [3]. During the experiment the camera was placed on a tripod and 35 mm lens was used on it. This high speed imaging system allows the researchers to record the machine in various conditions. In post processing authors used state of the art image processing system which is also used for example for measuring the speed of an opening airbag. This software is able to track characteristic points (Fig. 4) within the recorded frame and measure their relative movement, speeds and accelerations accordingly to the setup reference. During the testing phase numerous recordings were created and two specific scenarios were tested. The first scenario consisted of regular demolition work with use of hydraulic breaker. The machine had at least three points of support and was standing firmly on the ground. During the visit to the site researchers noticed that the operator of the machine for quicker chipping off the concrete sets up the machine in a way were it is standing only on rear supports and on the tip of the hydraulic breaker. Therefore it has been decided that the second researched scenario is going to be investigating the movement of the arm system when the concrete is chipped off and the machine loses stability until it falls on the front supports. Based on that scenario a theory was created that the crack growth might be caused by high stresses occurring when large mass of the breaker moves uncontrollably on a long arm during the chipping off process.

Fig. 4

Points in which the relative movement during the post process was measured

Besides the measurement using the high speed imaging system the authors used a vibrometer. This measurement allowed us to gauge the displacements of the certain points on the arm system in the frequency domain as well collect data about natural frequencies of the system in operation. This data was used in validation of the simulation model.

## 4 Simulation Model

Numerical model of the arm system was prepared using Siemens NX PLM software. This software consists of different modules which allowed authors to prepare and analyze the model within one software without the need to convert the file format in order to exchange the files between different programs. Geometrical model of the arm assembly was simplified in comparison to real life solution. This step assured authors that computational time will be reduced due to lowered number of finite elements and simpler model in the simulation. NX CAD software was used for simplification and creation of geometrical model (Fig. 5). At the computer model designing process authors decided to used midplane shell model for the arm representation. For the purposes of analyses it was sufficient and produced meaningful results along with significantly reduced computational time. The model was created using 7 different parts. Each one of those part was meshed separately in NX Nastran simulation module [4]. Brokk 90 arm is built from S355 steel [5], therefore simulation model was created using material with the same mechanical properties to achieve result corresponding with reality.

Fig. 5

Geometry created using Siemens NX CAD

Thickness of each component in the arm system varies due to different loadings acting on those parts. During numerical model creation this was taken into consideration and finite elements in individual parts had different thickness values assigned (Presented in Fig. 6) [6]. Components such as hydraulic breaker and hydraulic cylinders were simplified as well during the process of simulation model creation [7, 8]. Authors decided to use simple 1D finite elements with rod and hollow cylinder properties assigned to them. Hydraulic breaker was replaced by a concentrated point mass of 145 kg, which is the weight of the breaker, placed in the center of mass of a real hydraulic breaker.

Fig. 6

Variation of sheet metal thicknesses in the simulation model

### 4.1 Results of the Experiment

Authors decided to analyze one case which occurred during arm system testing and which in authors opinion has the highest impact on the assembly structure. This case shows a condition during which hydraulic breaker manages to remove part of the concrete from solid block. The operator sets the machine in a way that it is standing on the two supports in the back of the driving unit and the third support is the tip of the breaker. In this case the operator is able to use entire mass of the robot to achieve faster forging of concrete. When part of the concrete is removed due to work of the hydraulic breaker the machine loses one of three supports. Therefore it loses stability, when it is no longer supported on the tip of the breaker. Vibrations of entire arm system are showing when this state occurs. Course of movement, velocity and acceleration graphs for this particular case obtained while analyzing the high speed recording are shown on Fig. 7. The graphs corresponds to motion along Y axis. Analyzing the graphs it is visible where Brokk 90 lost stability during operation. At time of 600 ms accelerated movement of hydraulic breaker in Y axis is started. Based on the information gathered on the graph about velocities and accelerations acting on Brokk 90 arm system authors designed a worst case scenario for the simulation. Input boundary condition for simulation file would be velocity extortion over time. Authors decided to set boundary condition for a worst case scenario of velocity extortion which in this case would be 520 mm/s over time of 70 ms [8, 9].

Fig. 7

Course of movement of the tip of the boom while chipping off concrete

### 4.2 Results of the Simulation

Simulation was performed using NX Nastran solver, which is high end, state of the art finite element analysis software. The geometrical model was prepared for simulation. Boundary conditions were set based on results from high speed camera recording. Because driving unit of the Brokk 90 was not simulated therefore damping occurring through it could not be calculated. A simplification was established that base of the arm system is fully constrained to the ground—all 6° of freedom fixed. Results from finite element simulation are shown on Fig. 8.

Fig. 8

Results of the simulation of the arm system under loading

Maximum Huber-von Mises stresses are showing on the top shelf of the second member of the Brokk 90 arm system. Maximum stresses in this case are 163 MPa where fractures of real solution are appearing (Fig. 9). Stresses are below yield point for the material from which the arm is constructed but operation conditions that this kind of robot operates under need to be taken into consideration. No specific durability or fatigue simulation was performed. Authors presume that due to a fact that arm system is under constant percussive loading, it can cause microstructure fractures which will weaken the construction of the assembly significantly.

Fig. 9

Maximum stresses on the second section of the arm system

Additional validation of the simulation model was performed using the results obtained with help of the digital vibrometer Commtest vb7. Natural frequencies of the two systems, real life arm system and simulation model are presented in the Table 1.

## 5 Conclusions

The methodology used in this article proved to be useful in the case of investigating a demolition machine. Use of noninvasive methods allowed the researchers to perform quick and accurate measurements without necessity of putting the machine out of order for longer period of time. Recording with the high speed camera and later post processing allowed to obtain accurate values for the boundary conditions for the simulation. Data collected via measurements with vibrometer were used for final simulation model verification. Due to high level of correlation between real life data and simulation model the model has been proven valuable for future research. Authors of this work plan to use this model in the future, during the development of improved boom solution. The new design will not be vulnerable to the specific type of vibrations that cause previous design to fail before overhaul of the machine.

# Study Optimization of the Design-Construction Process of the Design Element of the Electric Remote Control Demolition Machine Based on the Design Thinking Methodology

Damian Derlukiewicz1  and Katarzyna Mielniczyn2

(1)

Department of Machine Design and Research, Wrocław University of Technology, Lukasiewicza 7/9, 50-371 Wroclaw, Poland

(2)

Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Wrocław University of Technology, Lukasiewicza 7/9, 50-371 Wroclaw, Poland

Damian Derlukiewicz (Corresponding author)

Email: damian.derlukiewicz@pwr.edu.pl

Katarzyna Mielniczyn

Email: kasia.mielniczyn@gmail.com

Abstract

All the machines that are used in various sectors of the machine industry are usually the work of the team which consists of many specialized people. Generally the final effect is evaluated which is the physically produced machine that people can see, touch and use. In fact, no one realizes how much effort and work is needed to make the team successfully complete the design of the machine and start the long-awaited final stage which is the manufacturing. Each machine before the start of manufacturing passes through the stages of design and construction. It should be noted that these steps are one of the most important in the whole process of the manufacture of machinery.

## 1 Introduction

All the machines that are used in various sectors of the machine industry are usually the work of the team which consists of many specialized people. Generally the final effect is evaluated which is the physically produced machine that people can see, touch and use. In fact, no one realizes how much effort and work is needed to make the team successfully complete the design of the machine and start the long-awaited final stage which is the manufacturing. Each machine before the start of manufacturing passes through the stages of design and construction. It should be noted that these steps are one of the most important in the whole process of the manufacture of machinery.

In the following part of the article, there is a description of the design-construction process in the existing literature which is an important point of reference for the development of a new scheme for design-construction process. The new scheme was mainly based on the assumptions of the methodology of Design Thinking which involves the creation of innovative design products based on deep understanding of the problems and needs of users. The main aim of this article is to present all stages of the new scheme of design-construction process on the example of the improved three-piece hydraulic arm of the electric remote- controlled demolition machine.

## 2 Conventional Design-Construction Process

Designing in technology is called a creative activity with a certain share of routine work. It can affect both new and upgraded products. In fact, designing is the formation of new concepts (solutions) of the product which can be thought of as creative processes, so-called innovations. The main task of the modern preparation of new concepts (projects) is to isolate issues of designing, as an intermediate step between the research and the manufacturing.

The design-construction process proceeds variously depending on whether constructing a completely new machine or upgrading existing [5]. Prior to manufacturing, a full documentation of the machine should be prepared, including design documentation. For the new machine designing process begins based on assumptions which are about the main parameters and requirements of the machine. The designer begins his work by gathering information about so far made solutions of similar machines because it allows to use a little of existing experiences. The designer should also refer to the existing patents which may prevent the use of certain solutions. During designing a new machine it is also necessary to make the preliminary design. It contains: a description of major groups of the machine, a functional calculations, a preliminary bill of materials, kinematic diagrams etc. At this stage designer should think about possible alternatives and conduct the selection from the point of view of the optimization of the machine.

The tasks of the designer during designing of the machine are as follows [4]:

  * selection of the kinematic scheme,

  * identification of power and selection of motor,

  * designing parts,

  * designing assemblies,

  * determination of kinematic and dynamic parameters,

  * functional and dynamic calculations.

On the other hand, during constructing, the shape, dimensions, material and technology of the parts are set. The tasks of the constructor [4, 5]:

  * determination the shapes and dimensions of the parts in such a way that they fulfill their tasks,

  * selection of the material for parts,

  * determination, in general, manufacturing technology,

  * determination of surface treatment, surface roughness, galvanized coating etc.

  * determination of heat treatment of parts (hardening, annealing, quenching etc.)

The conventional scheme of design-construction process is shown in Fig. 1.

Fig. 1

The conventional scheme of design-construction process [4]

## 3 Design Thinking—The Definition and Stages

Classical schemes of the design-construction process do not contain stages about getting to know the problems and needs of the future user of designed product. Thanks to an innovative methodology—Design Thinking—there is a possibility to meet the user's requirements about the product.

Design Thinking is a methodology of creating innovative products and services based on deep understanding of the problems and needs of users. The assumptions of this methodology are primarily about focus on the user—understanding of his conscious and unconscious needs. During designing, the interdisciplinary team is needed. This team helps to look at the problem from different perspectives. The essence of Design Thinking is primarily experimentation and frequent testing of hypotheses by building simple prototypes and collecting feedback from users about the product. The overall objective of Design Thinking is the creation and implementation of innovative solutions, including new products, services, innovative technologies, processes, educational programs and even business models. Regardless of the site of action (business, industry, education etc.), Design Thinking promotes innovation and provides original solutions.

The stages of Design Thinking, as shown in Fig. 2, are [1]:

Fig. 2

Stages of Design Thinking [1]

  1. (1)

Empathize—"entry in the user's skin". It is a deep understanding of the needs and problems of the user. To identify hidden and intuitive users motivation are used ethnographic interviews, map of empathy, observations and exploratory surveys with a detailed analysis of the environment and needs in terms of functionality.

  2. (2)

Define—during this stage the team makes synthesis of the information gathered during the stage "empathize" to determine the correct problem. This stage requires breaking frameworks of thought and habits which limit opportunities to explore new solutions. A proper definition of the problem will accurately determine the direction for new solutions.

  3. (3)

Ideate—a stage, wherein the team is focused on generating many possible solutions for the specifically defined problem. It is important to create new and original solutions. The main tool in this step is brainstorming.

  4. (4)

Prototype—in this stage, a physical prototype is built. The aim is not to create complicated models, only those with characteristics similar to the final product. As a result, there is a possibility of practical presentation of the idea to users and rapid feedback on the solution. This may reduce the risk of a final failure. To build simple prototypes, it can be anything: cardboard, wood, sheet of paper etc. Generally, it is important to take a step further than a verbal description. It is a lot better to make visual introduction of new idea.

  5. (5)

Test—this stage is about testing the solution in user's environment. It requires an enormous commitment of many people and support from the technical, formal and legal aspects. After the completed tests, the result is evaluated. If it is positive, then the product or service is ready for final implementation. Unfortunately, the stage of testing is often overlooked during the implementation of many projects. The seemingly good ideas and solutions are immediately put into everyday use and then it turns out that they do not meet the basic requirements, assumptions and expectations of the users.

## 4 The Electric Remote-Controlled Demolition Machine—The Description and the Visualization

Currently for demolition works the electric remote-controlled demolition machines are being used. Their advantage is that they can work in confined and dangerous areas to people. Their small size allows to work in the tunnels and in the interior of demolished buildings.

The most popular manufacturer of electric remote-controlled demolition machines is the Brokk. Currently, the company offers the following models of demolition machines: Brokk 60, Brokk 100, Brokk 160, Brokk 260, Brokk 400, Brokk 400 Diesel, Brokk 800 Brokk 800 Process and Standard. By 2013, the company had been manufacturing other types of robots: Brokk 50, Brokk 90 etc. In this article, it will appear the construction of the robot Brokk 90 because the optimization of the design-construction process will be applied to the three-piece hydraulic arm of this robot.

Brokk 90 is electro-hydraulic remote-controlled demolition machine. It is one of the most versatile tools on the market for demolition in confined spaces. Picture of the robot is shown in Fig. 3. Its key features include:

Fig. 3

The electric remote-controlled demolition machine—Brokk 90 [2] (1—three-piece hydraulic arm, 2—support stiffeners, 3—tools, 4—housing)

  * low weight (1015 kg),

  * compact construction for ease of transport (height—1219 mm, width—780 mm),

  * great maneuverability,

  * high power—11 kW

  * combination of a small area of contact with the ground and rubber tracks which minimize vibration for construction and allow user to work on narrow structures,

  * ability to adapt in hot environment, such as cement kilns, steel mills and other applications.

## 5 Optimization of Design and Construction Process Based on the Tree-Part Hydraulic Arm of Electrical Working Machine

Arcad company based in Wroclaw uses in construction demolition among other the BROKK robot—specifically model Brokk 90. After a few years of use of the robot there were problems with the strength of a three-part arm system. After many attempts to improve the structure of the arm, the company decided to create its own design of improved arm member of specialized demolition machines. The process of design and construction arm was created using the Design Thinking methodology. Diagram showing all stages of design and construction is shown in Fig. 4. This is a general algorithm for creating design of a new product for which the company Arcad will be able to build in the future while creating other products.

Fig. 4

General scheme of the design-construction process based on the methodology of design thinking

The design process of the hydraulic three-part arm of an electrical working machine starts from some external factor, which is the internal company development. All feedback related to the progress of the project are directed to the company owner Arcad. The next step is to identify the tasks of the project, which leads to the creation of specialized interdisciplinary project team for the working machine arm to create an appropriate work schedule for the design and assessment of the duration of the project.

Next steps are: empathy, understanding of the problem, to define the real problem, generating solutions and their evaluation, to build simple prototypes and selection of the best concepts. These steps are taken from the Design Thinking methodology and largely determine the success of the whole project. The result of empathy of a new three-piece hydraulic arm of the electric machine is to change the structure of the arms and their material in relation to the robot arm Brokk 90. What is also important is the feedback to the ARCAD owner, which may at any time, express his positive or negative opinion on the draft. After selecting the best concepts of the arm it is necessary to create project plan documents for the management board and wait for the decision. A management decision can be positive or negative. A negative decision may be associated with an improvement of project plan or complete rejection of the project. After a positive decision of the board the preliminary design is created.

Next steps are closely related to the design of a product. These stages include 3D design and detailed design, after which every time you need to carry out a thorough verification [3]. After verification of the detailed design, you can go straight to deploy to production or to create a detailed three-part prototype hydraulic arm of the electric working machine, carry on the research and then implement into production. The process of design and construction ends on the implementation in the production, because this stage is closely related to the physical form of the product according to the previously established technology.

## 6 Conclusions

Integration of the design-construction process with the stages of Design Thinking methodology enables to improve the proper and better understanding the user, in this case machine operator, needs. By using the methodology of Design Thinking during the design and construction it is possible to prevent a situation that appears most frequently in the presentation of physically produced final product when a customer says, "Quite differently I imagined this product. It does not meet my expectations." The conventional scheme of design-construction process starts with gathering information about new solution or redesigned product, that are defined by the designer or product manager. Often the designing process begins based on assumptions which are about the main parameters and requirements of the machine, that do not include the real problem solving of the user. Implementation of design thinking methodology allows to understand the user need and also define the real problem that must be faced with.

The above-mentioned stages of elaborated innovative design and construction process have been used to describe the project of remotely controlled demolition robot in ARCAD company. Versatility of created schema allows its use to create other projects in the future. The study indicates how important role in the design and construction process of the product plays a good relationship with the customer.

# The Numerical-Experimental Studies of Demolition Machine Operator Work

Damian Derlukiewicz1  , Mariusz Ptak1  , Johannes Wilhelm2  and Krzysztof Jakubowski3

(1)

Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Department of Machine Design and Research, Wrocław University of Science and Technology, Lukasiewicza 7/9, 50-371 Wroclaw, Poland

(2)

Brandenburg University of Technology (BTU) Cottbus – Senftenberg, Platz der Deutschen Einheit 1, 03046 Cottbus, Germany

(3)

ARCAD Ltd, Stargardzka 7-9, 54-156 Wrocław, Poland

Damian Derlukiewicz

Email: damian.derlukiewicz@pwr.edu.pl

Mariusz Ptak (Corresponding author)

Email: mariusz.ptak@pwr.edu.pl

Johannes Wilhelm

Email: johannes.wilhelm@pwr.edu.pl

Krzysztof Jakubowski

Email: krzysztof.jakubowski@arcad.wroc.pl

Abstract

A demolition robot is a multi-functional, remote-controlled machine, which is designed to be operated in severe work conditions such as high temperature, dust, radiation or noise. The publication presents the approach to enhance both the robustness of the machine—through Finite Element optimization—and the ergonomics of machine operator by implementing Human-Machine Interface (HMI). The combination of performed experimental and numerical research provided the information about the unfavorable effort and frequency states of the machine in the various operation processes. The use of advanced numerical simulations in pair with experimental tests were applied to estimate the dangerous states of the structure of the machine, as the designing stage enables to elaborate the HMI warning control system of the machine operation.

Keywords

Demolition robotHMI (Human-Machine Interface)Conceptual designResonant frequencyFEM (Finite element Method)Human-controlled machines

## 1 Introduction

Cities around the world are continuously evolving, so there is an unrelenting demand for specialists in demolition, capable in a professional way to remove unneeded property and prepare a place for new investments. Due to high risk to civilians, lack of documentation, nearby surrounding elements or just partial renovation some buildings in city centers cannot be destroyed using explosives—they must be demolished.

The demolition is a process more costly, time-consuming and demanding strict planning. This in turn brings to the need to maximize the efficiency of all kinds of works. At the same time it is increasingly important due to workplace health and safety (WHS). Therefore, some traditional methods—including physical workers equipped with hammers and pickaxes, or operators of excavators—are not further feasible.

To meet the high demands, there are many new technical solutions—the demolition robots are getting more popular recently. These mobile machines are usually operated remotely, making the operator's work easier and more ergonomic. The robots often replace the heavy equipment, especially when there is not enough space for safe operation of conventional excavators. By varying the size, demolition can be lead both outside facilities, as well as in areas where access is through door openings with a width of 80 cm. Moreover, unlike the workers they do not get tired or even bored repeating the same operations every day. Usually, they have a working range beyond human abilities, and most importantly, they can be used in places dangerous to men.

Besides a number of advantages, there are also drawbacks resulting from the use of demolition robots, mainly that depend on their reliability. As long as the company uses the manufacturer's authorized service robot, it can count on the fact that in the event of a major accident will be made available to the robot replacement. However, if the device is old, or the company decides to service the machines on their own, the consequences of failure can be disastrous. Assuming that the company has one robot, each of its failure could mean a break in the schedule of work, which in many cases may result in delay of work so large that the principal has applied penalties. That is why it is so important to reduce the number of major accidents on construction of robots to a minimum.

ARCAD Ltd. experienced some problems with the cracking one of the elements of the operating arm used in robotic demolition. Because it was not a one-time event, but recurring, it was decided to carry out some experimental and numerical tests, aimed at analyzing the structure of the robot and robot's arm. The results, when confronted with the results of Finite Element Analysis, will identify the causes of this breakdown. Figure 1 depicts the arm of the robot which was subjected to the research.

Fig. 1

Schematic view of a demolition robot arm: 1 base, 2 beam #1, 3 beam #2, 4 beam #3, 5 shields, 6 connectors, 7 actuators

## 2 Methodology

The studies consist of both experimental and numerical testing of demolition machine structure. The experimental testing was performed with the use of high-speed camera Phantom V12 (Fig. 2) in order to obtain the acceleration spectra of selected points during the machine operation. Two situations were arbitrary chosen as the most common states during demolition works i.e.: proper demolition, where an operator uses full capacity of the hammer versus improper work, whilst the hammer is either not in the material or in the material which has been already demolished and the hammer is not proceeding towards its solid part.

Fig. 2

High-speed camera recording during on-site tests: real view (left); footage from Phantom V12 (right) analyzed by TEMA Motion with a marker point #1

The results of the high-speed camera were analyzed by TEMA Motion, which allowed the generation of waveforms of displacement, velocity and acceleration of points located on the arm during operation (Fig. 2). The data was compared to the studies, where the vibrometer was used [1].

The use of a high-speed camera provided valuable data concerning the acceleration of special, pre-defined points on the demolition robot. To get more information out of the recorded data as shown in the time graph below (Fig. 3), a FFT power spectrum also by using National Instruments LabVIEW was performed. While the time graph visualises the vertical acceleration for certain time, the power spectrum answers the question of how much of a concerned signal is at a frequency ω and reveals thereafter information about certain values like natural and demolition frequency itself (Fig. 4). The variation of the amplitude and power spectrum will aid the HMI system for informing an operator about working in improper condition, which may lead to the failure of the machine.

Fig. 3

Acceleration runs (vertical axis) for marker point #1: proper versus improper usage of the hammer

Fig. 4

Power spectrum from the recorded acceleration: proper versus improper usage of the hammer

The data obtained from experimental testing with high-speed camera were used for appliance of real life boundary conditions to the numerical model. Based on this data dynamic extortion acting on the working arm was applied. The analysis of numerical model was carried out in NX Nastran. Basing on 3D CAD model of demolition robot a computational model was further constructed. First stage of creating discretized model was to create geometrical model of the arm system. Members of arm systems used for construction machines, therein demolition machines, are thin body elements, so therefore authors decided to create thin shell model [2, 3] which is depicted in Fig. 5. In order to simulate hydraulic breaker SB152 the authors decided to replace it with 140 kg point mass. The model is solved with Lanczos method and then natural vibratory frequencies and modal vibratory models are obtained, which lays a basis for further dynamic analysis.

Fig. 5

Finite element model with contour thickness map in (mm)

The biggest stress resulting from vibrations of the model are obtained for frequency of 89 Hz. The maximum value of Huber-Mises-Hencky (H-M-H) stress in this case about 20 MPa (Fig. 6).

Fig. 6

H-M-H stress map (MPa) of the robot arm for the frequency of 89 Hz

Higher stresses can also be found on the top shelf of the second arm member of the arm system. Maximum H-M-H stress acting on arm members is 20 MPa. The stress does not exceed maximum yield strength of the material. However, it has to be noted that impact nature of hydraulic breakers works causes fatigue fracture of steel elements of arm members as it was already mentioned.

## 3 Human-Machine Interface

Demolition robots are mainly used in hazardous environments such as deconstruction areas of undocumented buildings and even nuclear-wasted constructions. In such a situation, there is no direct connection between worker and machinery. This gain of safety for human beings on the one hand is in fact a loss of feedback given by the machine itself related to its working conditions and situations on the other hand. Undoubted, this knowledge is as well crucial for the operator to control a heavy machine like a demolition robot without risking damages to it and makes a human-machine interface obligatory.

While an optical based HMI could be concealed or hidden by the arm of the robot itself and an acoustic based system could be drown out by general noise annoyance, the creation of a haptic force-feedback system implemented in the operator's manipulator represents itself as an conceivable iteration of the feedback system according to the robot's and operator's safety. Especially, because there are concepts, that predict that "The hand looks faster than the eye." [4, 5].

### 3.1 Haptic FF

Force Feedback is based on haptic. The word haptic has its origin in the Greek haptikos, from haptesthai, to grasp or touch, which is nowadays defined by the sense of touch. In computer-based haptics this ability to feel is related to a peripheral device, the so called force-feedback-device, which performs with a force e.g. on the finger or the hand of the user to pretend the existence of a mechanical connection and the feedback of a subsystem or a single force [4] and is clearly concentrated to the idea of direct interaction between man and machine. Forms of these interactions were able to be found as well in entertainment electronics, in several remote-controlled devices as even in modern planes and show a direct or indirect force feedback behaviour.

As an example of indirect force feedback the Accelerator Force Feedback Pedal (AFFP) was invented and introduced by Continental AG as an active gas pedal with an integrated actuator to serve the driver with special information about the actual driving situation. This feedback is given to the driver by a vibrating gas pedal. Such information is thought as an advice like getting off the foot from the gas pedal for optimizing the gasoline consumption or to reducing the car speed for setting the safety distance to a preceding vehicle [6]. Recapitulatory and related to the robot's HMI, this system provides a feedback concerning a single circumstance. Instead of acting against an external force as the push of the control stick, it indicates by shaking or vibrating the harming usage of the whole system robot. Beside this, the intention of such a system as the AFFP is to get a faster and quicker response to and from the user of the system, as compared to conventional solutions, using just optical and acoustic components.

The main negative aspect of an indirect force-feedback system as a conceivable additional, external device with a small hazard of failure exists in the circumstance, that a vibrating device is decreasing in every case the ability of controlling the robot safely and highly accurate, while the hazard of doing unwanted movements with the robot caused by the vibrations increases unacceptably.

In contrast to the previously pointed solutions, direct force feedback-devices act indeed with a counterforce inverted to the direction of an applied force or momentum, for example the movement of a joystick of the manipulator. The counterforce will be applied by an actuator, e.g. a small electric motor coupled to the application. In the result, here the user experience will be extended by an increased or decreased resistance to the operator's controlling action in the same axis. The example of multi-direction force feedback is realised by University of Nagoya's Virtual Endoscope System for the purpose of training medical personnel for non-invasive and low-invasive techniques of diagnosis and surgery, especially by using an endoscope and is shown in Figs. 7 and 8.

Fig. 7

Compact force display mechanism using ball drive mechanism (VES-IV) [7]

Fig. 8

Feedback device of the portable virtual endoscope system [7]

The VES drive mechanism shown in Fig. 8 is a decoupled ball drive mechanism consisting mainly of four electric motors with affixed rollers. These assemblies are located 90° to each other and framing a rubber ball. With this rubber ball it is possible to drive the rubber ball contacted endoscope in linear motion and even in rotation, which allows in the complete application to generate force information beside the visual information shown on a screen while the training for diagnosis and surgery.

By thinking about the realisation of a direct force feedback system in the demolition robots' remote controller to express the robots state of being misused, overpowered or used within the natural frequency it is clear, that the adaption can be easily done only for one direction or axis as a single push-button. The effort rises by demands of multi-axis–feedback and reliability. Also effects like slip of the rubber ball referred to the actuators will have to be considered by designing the possible remote controller. The installation of such a direct force feedback system is further on not possible as an extension.

Nevertheless, using a direct force feedback system can give the operator a special feedback equal to the value of overpowering in the axis of user-applied force on the manipulator, which involves the operator obviously in the most natural way for a remote controlled machine. In the example of PHANToM, a haptic device enabling the user to feel a three-dimensional item, only non-real existing in a computer's memory, a peak maximum of 10 N of counterforce is mentioned [8]. Furthermore, a system acting based on a counterforce will not affect the sensitivity and accuracy as hard as a vibrating device.

### 3.2 Non-haptic

However, in several situations and customer wishes the usage of a non-haptic interface to inform about the existence or even the level of a supervised, acting force is inescapable. Hereafter related to the present iteration of a demolition robot [1], a non-haptic feedback device will be introduced, that could be adapted to the present iteration of the demolition robot. The idea of this possible device is based on one important part of the whole operating system, all robots have in common: an operator with helmet, safety googles and (circumaural) ear protection, which is widely classified furthermore as personal safety gear of workers. Each of these parts is due to safety regulations in working environments obligatory and accomplishes a list of tasks, mainly to protect head, eyes and ears from injuries due to airborne items, collisions with static obstacles and noise level. By also fulfilling the additional tasks of carrying an accumulator and Bluetooth communication device within the helmet, illuminating the light-conductor framed shield (Fig. 9) in case of a supervised event and signalling it furthermore acoustically within the ear protection, which acts in this case as a headphone, the realisation of a multi-part non-haptic feedback device with this safety equipment could be done.

Fig. 9

Concept of a feedback-helmet system

The shown wireless system reduces in this case not only the hazard of injuries like strangulation due to using tethered components, furthermore it improves worker's safety with a pre-defined noise level. By installing a headphone inside the ear protection, a warning signal noise level-situated in a safe range and related to the noise level of the working environment itself can be aspired. This is as well convenient to reduce the noise annoyance of the working environment generally and covers an up-to-the-minute topic in environmental emission concerns.

## 4 Conclusions

The aim of the paper was to prevent the operation of the demolition machine in unfavorable conditions. The experimental testing with high-speed camera and vibrometer was performed to obtain the input data for numerical analysis. The result in form of the acceleration runs recorded during two cases of machine operation (proper and improper) provided the spectrum of frequencies, that significantly indicates the difference in operation. For the proper use of the hammer the amplitude of power spectrum is in the range up to max 200 m/s2 where at the improper operation the amplitude increases up to 600 m/s2. That shows the possibility of use of power spectrum for human machine interface, as the indication system of proper working operation of the machine. This kind of system can be applied in feedback based helmet system. The helmet system notifies the operator about the load capacity and warns the operator about leading the arm in resonant frequency, which is a main cause of the reported robot's arm fatigue failure.

Demolition robot, in particular, examined the arm system working during operation, is constantly exposed to the presence of oversized loads, threatening its reliability. On the one hand, this is one of the important aspects why robots are used- that an operator does not have to work in hazardous conditions.

With our results of numerical calculations can be quickly and does not require prototypes to verify, as designed structure will work in extreme conditions. This study showed the conditions of machine operation, that can be dangerous as far as the construction strength and fatigue life is concerned. This, in turn, causes the construction cracking during the improper operation like hammering.

The comparison of the experimental and numerical study enabled the authors to propose such a type of warning HMI system, that could be applied to the operation process, which bases on the power spectrum measurements.

Further elaborated algorithms, that base on the power spectra differences, can be implemented in force feedback system, that act on the operator via helmet-feedback- or remote control-systems.

# The Impact of Cross Beam on Stresses of Girders in Low Water Bridges

Artur Duchaczek1

(1)

General Tadeusz Kosciuszko Military Academy of Land Forces, Czajkowskiego Street 109, 51-150 Wrocław, Poland

Artur Duchaczek

Email: aduchaczek@poczta.wp.pl

Abstract

Low water bridges are classified to a group of military bridges, most frequently made of materials obtained at their construction site (steel sections and wood). They are characterised by similar structural solutions as civilian bridges, commonly called detour or temporary ones. However, low water bridges are structures that are not expected to enable the conduct of shipping and the runoff of ice floes. The aim of this study is to determine the impact of the number of cross beams and their rigidity as well as assembly connections made on the stress distribution in spans of low water bridges. The carried out numerical analyses (FEM) have shown that either the number of girders or the number of cross beams significantly affect the stress distribution in main girders. Moreover, these analyses have proved that the rigidity of cross beams and the manner of assembly connections execution with the sufficiently rigid wood plate have little effect on the stress distribution in the major structural elements of low water bridges. The analyses have shown, however, a very large impact of the way of modelling assembly connections in a steel grate on the stress distribution in the wood plate.

## 1 Introduction

Low water bridges are simple engineering structures intended for short-term use, the design of which does not allow the conduct of shipping and the runoff of ice floes [5, 6]. In constructions of this type, screw connectors are used above all for joining single main girders made of steel I beams and channel sections. The number of cross beams when constructing low water bridges is defined based on empirical formulas, which subject their number to the span length and the type of the section type [3].

In handbooks on the design of military low water bridges strength calculations of spans are limited primarily to the correctly selected number and the cross-section of main girders [3]. Therefore, one of the objectives of this study (Phase I) was to determine the influence of the adopted supporting structure of low water bridges on the distribution of stresses in their main structural elements [1].

When analysing the existing screw connections in constructions of this type it seems that these connections cannot be completely rigid. Given that cross beams have no direct contact with the web of the main girder it may be assumed that in numerical calculations this type of connection should not be treated as perfectly stiff.

It may also be questionable whether the applied fairly flexible (less rigid) cross beams in relation to main girders are able to satisfactorily distribute the load on all girders located in the span [1, 2]. In practice, it is mainly provided by the concrete bridge slab. The question arises, however, how rigid should cross beams be in case of using the wood cross plate in such structures, which is the most versatile solution for the construction of military bridges in crisis situations.

For this reason, in this work in the second part of the study there was analysed the impact of rigidity changes in the adopted numerical calculations of assembly connections, as well as rigidity of cross beams, on the distribution of stresses in main girders of military low water bridges [2].

## 2 The Adopted Construction of the Low Water Bridge and Its Load

The analysis of technical parameters of tanks used by the Polish Armed Forces has shown that the combat mass of these vehicles is between 36.50 ÷ 59.50 tonnes [1]. Then, when analysing the weight of standard vehicles presented in STANAG 2021 [8] it was concluded that the vehicles, which the Polish Armed Forces are equipped with have similar dimensions to those of MLC40 ÷ MLC70 classes. Therefore, the MLC70 class tracked load was assumed as the design load. Vehicles of this class are characterised by the total weight of 63.50 tonnes, the width (at the track level) of 3.51 m, the track width of 0.79 m and the length of the track adhesion equal to 4.57 m [8].

Furthermore, the provisions of STANAG-2021 regulate the crossing of both wheeled and tracked vehicles over bridges. This document sets out the minimum required width of the road on which vehicles of relevant classes are to convey. Considering the fact that under the conditions of war and crisis situations low water bridges are better to be performed as unidirectional passages it was recognised that the most frequently used bridges would be the 4.00 m wide ones [1]. Taking the above considerations into account, for further analyses there was assumed a span of six main girders made of normal steel beams INP 400 (grade 355 steel) of the length of 14 m and the width of the road equal to 4.00 m.

In the first phase of the study the supporting steel structure of the low water bridge was modelled as a grate using 2-node rod finite elements. In this part of the study, the effects of the wood plate rigidity were not taken into consideration. However, in the second phase of the study the wood plate was additionally modelled as the coating construction with the aim to accurately determine the impact of the rigidity of cross beams on stresses in the main girders. When modelling the wood plate, there was applied the Coons meshing method using quadrilateral 4-node coating elements [4]. The wood plate was designed as a 10 cm thick plate made of C14 class wood.

In numerical calculations there was used the MLC70 class tracked vehicle being modelled as the L1 balanced load (the MLC70 tracked vehicle is located in the middle of the cross-section of the span) and the L2 unbalanced one (the MLC70 tracked vehicle is located at the curb), taking account of the small in this case eccentric arising from the difference in the width between the roadway and the vehicle. In this calculation, environmental loads, such as wind and snow, were not considered.

The option of the so-called 'moving load' was used in the strength calculations for determining parameters of the vehicle and the path of its movement along the analysed structure [4].

In the first phase of the study the load of the tracked vehicle (defined as the continuous (linear) load) was applied to the grate-type rod construction. This type of load had to be firstly replaced by 10 forces focused throughout the adopted load corresponding to the length of the track adhesion. However, when the concentrated force was not directly above the rod, the algorithm for its distribution among the next rods was applied.

In the second phase of the study the tracked vehicle was modelled with the surface load for the analysis of the rod-coating structure. This load is applied to a coating element as the contour load. In this option, the load was transmitted on the wooden section deck, and from there on the steel sections constituting support elements of the bridge structure.

## 3 The Impact of the Supporting Structure of the Girder on the Stress Distribution

In the first phase of the study there was analysed the impact of the amount of cross beams on the stress distribution in main girders. Here, the cross beams were modelled with H beams HEB200, also made of S355 grade steel.

With the tracked load set in the middle of the cross section of the span (L1) taken into calculations, it was found that, in general, together with the increase of the number of cross beams (cross members), stresses in main girders (Fig. 1a) as well as in the cross beams (Fig. 1c) decrease.

Fig. 1

The value of the maximum stress occurring in girders (a, b) and cross members (c, d) with the symmetric load L1 (a, c) and the asymmetric load L2 (b, d)

However, if the tracked load set at the maximum eccentricity (L2) is included in the calculations, the influence of the number of cross beams on the stress distribution in main girders cannot be unambiguously determined (Fig. 1b). Also in this case it was concluded that with the increase of the number of cross beams stresses in them decrease (Fig. 1d).

For both tracked load schemes (L1 and L2) it may be stated that the odd (7 items) number of girders beneficially influences the value of maximum stresses occurring therein (Fig. 1a, b). For the symmetric load scheme (L1) it was observed that with six girders the number of cross beams does not substantially affect the value of the maximum stress in the cross beams of the span analysed (Fig. 1c). Stress values in cross beams obtained for the schemes L1 and L2 differed significantly. It was also found that the smaller number of girders, the less stresses in the struts. This resulted from the positioning of the vehicle on the span, exactly from the distribution of concentrated forces (which modelled the MLC70 tracked vehicle) in relation to the cross sections.

When selecting the number of cross beams the economic aspect cannot be ignored. The increasing number of cross beams makes the girder heavier, which adversely affects the cost of its implementation, i.e. the purchase cost of steel sections.

## 4 The Impact of the Rigidity of Struts on the Stress Distribution in Main Girders

At the beginning of the second phase of the study the impact of the rigidity of cross beams on the stress distribution in main girders of low water bridges was analysed. The analyses included a span of six main girders and five rows of cross beams. For numerical analyses there were adopted cross beams made from three kinds of popular steel profiles, namely channel sections, normal beams as well as H beams. Steel sections adopted for numerical calculations were characterised by the height of the cross profile of 45–55% of the main girder. For numerical calculations it was assumed that all profiles are made of S355 grade steel.

The parameter most significantly affecting the strength of steel girders are the ratios of the bending strength W x. The analysis of the data contained in the standard [7] has shown that the increase in height of cross sections in each of the three analysed groups by 20 mm is followed by the growth of the bending strength W x at the level of 30%. The maximum difference in values of the bending strength W x can be specified for C180 channel sections and H-beams HEB220. In the present case, the H-beam is almost five times more 'resistant to bending' than the channel section.

Assuming that the 'rigidity of a rod' refers to the product of its moment of inertia I x and the Young's modulus E, it may be stated that the cross beams made of sections HEB220 are almost six times more 'rigid' than cross beams made of C180 sections.

Figure 2 shows the results of numerical calculations for the selected two computational schemes (L1 and L2), presenting stress values for main girders. Figure 2a displays the stress values arising from the L1 symmetric load, while Fig. 2b—from the L2 unbalanced load. For main girders there were given the maximum stress values in the most and the least loaded girders.

Fig. 2

The values of stresses in main girders of the span of the low water bridge arising from the a symmetric G1, b asymmetric G2 loads

The analysis of the results presented in Fig. 2 proves that in the case of the low water bridge construction 'rigidity of the cross beams' had little impact on the stress distribution in main girders. It can therefore be assumed that the wood plate, which had been adopted for calculations, appropriately distributed the load on the adjacent main girders.

Figure 3a presents the value of reduced stresses in the wood plate of the span of the low water bridge, coming from the MLC70 tracked vehicle load for both symmetric (L1) and unbalanced (L2) loads. In the case of the cross plate the reduced stress values were given in accordance with Huber-Misses hypothesis read from the central zone of the span. The analysis of the results presented does not allow the clear statement whether the rigidity of cross beams affects the value of stresses in the wood plate.

Fig. 3

The values of reduced stresses in the wood plate depending on the type of: a sections used for constructing cross beams, b the method of assembling cross beams made from C180 sections with main girders

## 5 The Impact of the Rigidity of Assembly Connections on the Stress Distribution in Main Girders

Further, the rigidity of assembly connections affecting the stress distribution in main girders required analyses. In this phase of the study the same span scheme as in Part 4 of this paper was adopted. Whereas the cross beams were modelled with normal channel sections of the height of 180 mm, made of S355 grade steel.

The DSC algorithm for calculating a structure with exemptions has been implemented in the programme Autodesk Robot Structural Analysis Professional. The use of the element DSC provides the definition of the so-called elastic exemptions in the rod elements [4].

For calculation purposes the advantage was taken of the option of the partial rigidity coefficient. The values of coefficients reducing rigidity can be ranging from 0.00 for the complete exemption to 1.00 for the total absence of the exemption. Thus, the value of the element rigidity is multiplied by the accepted value of the partial rigidity coefficient at the particular end of the rod [4].

Figure 4 presents the results of numerical calculations of the span in the low water bridge under the MLC70 class tracked load, considering different models of connections of steel elements. In numerical analyses there were included six types of connections, i.e. rigid ones, complete exemptions (i.e. articulated joints) and 20, 40, 60 and 80% exemptions using the coefficients reducing the rigidity available in the programme Autodesk Robot Structural Analysis Professional.

Fig. 4

The values of stresses in main girders of the low water bridge (for struts made from the C180 sections) arising from the: a symmetric L1, b asymmetric L2, loads

The diagrams below show stress values in main girders of the low water bridge arising from the MLC70 tracked vehicle load located at the mid-span L1 (Fig. 4a) and the MLC70 tracked vehicle load placed at the curb L2 (Fig. 4b).

The analysis of the results presented in Fig. 4 proves that in the case of the given construction of the low water bridge, the way of connecting struts with girders also slightly affected the stress distribution in the main girders. It can therefore be assumed that, as previously, the wood plate used for calculations properly distributed the load on the adjacent main girders.

The smaller thickness of the wood plate should not be implemented due to the fact that the cross plate is always determined on the basis of the wheeled, not tracked, load. Minimum dimensions of the cross plate should be 5 cm, while of the shelter plate 4–5 cm, giving in total 9–10 cm [3].

Figure 3b presents the value of the maximum reduced stresses in the wood plate of the low water bridge for struts made from the C180 section. It should be noted that the conducted analyses showed a very large impact of the way of modelling connections in the steel grate on the stress distribution in the wood plate. In relation to the span with articulated joints (the total exemption), the reduced stresses exceeded almost five times the value of stresses compared to the grate with rigid connections.

## 6 Conclusion

The analyses carried out in this work evidenced that both the number of girders and the number of cross beams significantly affect the stress distribution in the major structural elements of low water bridges. This means that omitting the number of cross beams in the process of selecting girders of low water bridges is a serious mistake and should be taken into account in the current textbook on designing military bridges.

On the basis of calculations conducted the conclusion can be drawn that for main girders made of steel beams, provided that their spacing does not exceed the distance of 0.80 m, the use of cross beams made of steel sections, which are about half the height of the main girder high, is sufficient.

Undoubtedly, the adopted calculation model for the grid supporting structure influenced the results of the numerical calculations. Assuming even minimum cooperation between the wood plate and steel girders it can be stated that the plate mounted on main girders contributes to changes of the section modulus coefficient of the whole cross-section of the span of the low water bridge. It causes stresses higher in lower tension fibres of main girders than in upper compressed ones.

Therefore, it is obvious that the adopted rod and rod-coating calculation models of the span of the low water bridge do not perfectly reflect the work of this type of construction, but they may illustrate the general character of work of the military bridge span. Due to the adopted calculation models of the supporting structure of bridges, the stability of the construction was not analysed in this work. The detailed analysis of the stability of the construction of the being discussed spans of low water bridges is going to be the subject of the forthcoming work.

# Analysis of the Test Rig Conception for the Drilling-Bolting Systems Testing

Paulina Działak1  and Jacek Karliński1

(1)

Department of Machine Design and Research, Wroclaw University of Science and Technology, Lukasiewicza 7/9, 50-371 Wroclaw, Poland

Paulina Działak (Corresponding author)

Email: paulina.dzialak@pwr.edu.pl

Jacek Karliński

Email: jacek.karlinski@pwr.edu.pl

Abstract

The paper presents preliminary design and analysis of the drilling-bolting rig, designed for testing the underground mining machines. Examination at the depth of 1000 m and deeper are almost impossible to perform due to the prevailing conditions. The authors designed the structure of the testing stand and carried out a strength analysis of the conceptual model of the rig. It resulted in a complete project of the test stand for drilling and bolting systems.

Keywords

Test standDrilling-bolting rigStrength analysisFEM

## 1 Introduction

The exploitation in the underground mines nowadays occurs at ever increasing depths, which clearly deteriorate the conditions prevalent in the mining excavation. The temperature of the machine operation environment is about 45° and flooding of the mine floors. Considering the geology, the area is characterized by ample lean angles in longitudinal and horizontal directions as well as by a relatively low headroom of the mine gallery. This region is strongly exposed to the unforeseeable rockbursts and rock falls [1]. Therefore, the implementation of the machines solely for testing in this area is very difficult and cost-consuming. For this reasons, the authors decided to design the test stand that will enable to verify the drilling and bolting systems of the underground mines without the necessity of introducing the machine to the excavation. The paper describes all the steps taken to obtain the complete model, prepared for production.

## 2 Aim and Scope of Research

The aim was to develop a methodology for a conceptual design and analysis [2] to create a model of the testing rig for the examination of the correct operation and reliability of the drilling and bolting machines [3]. The project was developed and verified with the use of the numerical modelling and simulation software [4]. The test stand will enable to test full processes of drilling and bolting with all its impediments. Usually, this type of systems perform numerous different functions from drilling the holes for the anchor bolts to assemble various kinds of the bolts [5]. Therefore, it is significant to verify all the parts of the process still on the surface, in the industrial conditions.

## 3 Conception the Test Stand

The model of the structure and the range of options of the testing rig was determined in accordance with the scope and the methodology of research. The test stand needs to enable the examination of all important operational functions of the drilling and bolting systems. It consists of four pillars fixed with a steel plate and bolts glued chemically to a reinforced concrete slab. Conceptual model of the rig project made of steel S3355 [6] is shown in Fig. 1.

Fig. 1

Conceptual design of the test stand for the drilling-bolting underground systems

## 4 Strength Analysis

To verify the strength of a carrying structure, finite element analysis (FEA) [7] of the testing rig model was performed. The numerical calculations of the loadings derived from lifting on a test stand a large rock solid box made of concrete or natural rock. Parameters of this box are similar to the rock mass existing in the underground mines [8], where the drilling process is carried out. The maximal mass of the box is equal 5000 kg due to strength of the structure.

The project encompassed following issues:

  * creating a 3D model of the test stand,

  * developing a technical documentation,

  * creating a surface geometry on the basis of a documentation,

  * defining a discrete model,

  * linear strength analysis of the structure in the static range,

  * analysis of the results.

On the basis of a 3D model created in Pro/Engineer software, surface geometry was developed and then discrete model of the test stand structure. Strength analysis was carried out with the use of a finite element method (FEM) [9].

First stage was to create the surface geometry of the structure, defining its outer shape. It was developed on the basis of the volume model and 2D documentation. Then, the geometry was used to create the discrete model of a testing rig. The FEM model consists of three- and four-node, thick-walled shell elements with 6 degrees of freedom in every node [10]. The average size of the element was 15 mm. Moreover, to develop full discrete model, beam, rigid and mass elements were used. The surface geometry is presented in Fig. 2. The discrete model with the boundary conditions defined for the analysis is shown in Fig. 3.

Fig. 2

Surface geometry of the testing rig for a drilling and bolting process

Fig. 3

The discrete model of the test stand with the defined boundary conditions

## 5 Results

The results of the simulation are presented in a graphical form of the contour lines of the stresses according to H-M-H hypothesis [11], in every point of the structure. The analysis was carried out with a simultaneous blockage of the working platform and support on the hydraulic actuators. The results of the calculations are shown in Figs. 4 and 5.

Fig. 4

Contour lines of the stresses according to H-M-H hypothesis

Fig. 5

Contour lines of the stresses according to H-M-H hypothesis (close-up)

## 6 Summary

The paper presents a method of the designing the conceptual testing rig that will enable to test reliability and correct operation of the underground drilling-bolting machines on the surface. Basing on the assumptions of the project, the geometrical and discrete models were developed. After imposing the boundary conditions to the virtual structure, strength analysis was performed. Discrete model of a test stand was loaded with a mass of the rock box equal 5000 kg. Simulation was carried out with a simultaneous blockage of the working platform and support on the hydraulic actuators. The calculations were conducted with use of finite element method. The result in form of the contour lines of the stresses according to H-M-H hypothesis were obtained.

In the analyzed case, the stress limit connected to the yield strength for the steel S355 (Re = 355 MPa) were not exceeded and the maximal stresses were less than 50% of the yield strength. This means that the safety factor was equal k = 2.

# Verification of the Theory of Construction Similarities in the Connectors

Piotr Gendarz1  , Rafał Rząsiński1  and Dominik Rabsztyn1

(1)

Gliwice, Poland

Piotr Gendarz

Email: piotr.gendarz@polsl.pl

Email: dominik.rabsztyn@polsl.pl

Abstract

Theory of construction similarity allows creating ordered construction families (series of types, modular construction systems). On the basis of the specific conditions of construction similarity and values of model characteristics, the parameter and dimension values have been determined. For the purpose of practical verification of the conditions of construction similarity the strength verification with MES and practical verification with a ripper have been performed. An attempt at practical verification of the construction similarity has been also performed using the ripper. The tests have been carried out with the use of threaded and welded joints and grippers. For that purpose, on the basis of conditions of construction similarity and dimensions of model construction, the construction series of types has been created.

## 1 Introduction

The theory of construction similarity allows creating ordered construction families (series of types, modular construction systems), where the element structure is characterized by the fixed construction form   [1–3]. ## 4 Results

An attempt at practical verification of the construction similarity has been also performed using the ripper. The tests have been carried out with the use of threaded and welded joints and grippers [9, 12].

For that purpose, on the basis of conditions of construction similarity and dimensions of model construction, the construction series of types has been created. Subsequently, the technology series of types has been developed that was further used as series of types. Construction features have been selected in a way that facilitated the maximum material stress, Fig. 7.

Fig. 9

Strength verification with the ripper

The basis for the result analysis was the critical force of frictional contact and destruction of the connections established on the basis of the construction similarity theory, Fig. 10.

Fig. 10

Results of the practical verification

The force P [kN] represents the force threshold transmitted by the connection, that resulted in the connection break. The force has also been determined analytically, which has been shown in Fig. 10.

It is noticeable that there is a deviation of the force threshold from the force determined analytically within the range of −19.36%. This means that the states have been relatively identical in the discussed threaded connections series of types created on the basis of construction similarity theory.
