# The Process of Parameterization and Creating Reference Construction

Piotr Gendarz1  , Rafał Rząsiński1  and Dominik Rabsztyn1

(1)

Institute of Engineering Processes Automation and Integrated Manufacturing Systems, Silesian University of Technology, Konarskiego Street 18a, 44-100 Gliwice, Poland

Piotr Gendarz

Email: piotr.gendarz@polsl.pl

Rafał Rząsiński (Corresponding author)

Email: rafal.rzasinski@polsl.pl

Dominik Rabsztyn

Email: dominik.rabsztyn@polsl.pl

Abstract

In the process of creating a series of types of construction, it is important to develop a reference construction that best meets the principles of construction and right of existence of technical product [1–3]. Construction of reference in the family construction can be selected from among existing structures or designed from the ground up as shown this publication. This is a construction practically verified in terms of its function (CAD simulation) and subject to optimization (particularly CAE strength optimization) that was verified due to the production (technology was developed in CAM) and the obtained product was subject to experimental verification (prototype tests).

## 1 Introduction

The purpose of using the theory of construction similarity is creating the ordered construction family such as types of series of construction on the basis of the reference construction Fig. 1.

Fig. 1

The series of types of construction created on the basis of the reference construction

As far as market economy is concerned, to construct elements not only to develop one construction of product, but it is advised to create a collection of constructions encompassing a wide range of demands for the specific class of products The idea of manufacturing, for instance, rod clevises only the load of P = 4kN, with the rod or piston diameter of d = M16 and the diameter of the hole for the coupling pin of D = 16 mm, Fig. 1, would result in a very little interest in such product. On the other hand, when we create the ordered construction family in the form of series of types of the rod clevises, for the set of demands identified by the unified characteristic features with the value range of: P = 0.9–8 kN, d = M5-M30, D = 5–30 mm, this will contribute to higher chances of acquiring a client and better adjustment to the client's needs, which also leads to better possibilities of staying on the competitive market. Therefore, it is justified to develop the construction methods, where on the basis of one construction a rational series of types with fixed construction form but variable dimension values is created. On that basis, quantitative and qualitative aspect comes down to the quantitative aspect, which means the problem of selecting the optimal values of dimensions   for the characteristic features  . This assignment, in the process of creating ordered construction families (series of types, modular construction systems) was called assignment γ [4–6],

(1)

In the construction similarity based method of creating ordered construction families, we distinguish the following stages:

  * selection, verification and modification of the reference construction,

  * unification and parameterization of the ordered construction family,

  * construction record with the open dimension layout,

  * creating the conditions of parameters and dimensions similarity,

  * calculation and verification of the dimension values of the elements series of types,

  * parametric construction record.

## 2 Reference Construction

A reference construction (ks0) is a construction practically verified in terms of its functionality (CAD simulation) and subject to optimization (particularly CAE strength optimization) that was verified due to the production (CAM systems) and the obtained product was subject to experimental verification (prototype tests). The construction may be accepted as the reference construction once its respective product successfully meets the criteria of the experimental verification. Due to the accuracy of calculations of dimension values using the construction similarity method it is advised to take the reference construction from the mid-range of the ordered parameter values. We distinguish two ways of creating reference constructions:

  * criteria-based selection from the collection of the existing constructions, that has already been the basis for production and the produced product satisfied the performance criteria,

  * using the Variation Analysis tool for the newly created reference construction.

In the first case, the purpose of selecting the reference construction is mainly specialization and extending the range of the products and the demand for a given class of products. First, the practical evaluation of the existing construction solutions is undertaken by the experts representing designers, construction engineers, technologists, economists, manufacturers, users and service specialists. Based on their opinions, it is possible to make the optimal choice or to modify the construction by creating the reference construction ks0. The example may be the chosen reference construction forms of glands used in hydraulic cylinders in the mining industry, Fig. 2a. The result of the criteria-based evaluation and selection are the construction solutions for glands, Fig. 2b. Applying the identical approach for the remaining systems of the cylinder, it was possible to create reference l construction forms of the hydraulic cylinders, Fig. 2c.

Fig. 2

Creating reference constructions of the hydraulic cylinders in the mining industry

A special tool for creating a reference construction for the newly created ordered construction family is using the Variation Analysis developed, for instance, in the advanced graphic software I-DEAS. The variation analysis uses the finite element method that is additionally extended by:

  * sensitivity analysis—relevant dimensions of the elements are chosen due to their strain, deformation conditions and mass,

  * parametric analysis—optimal values [7] are determined for the preset value ranges of relevant dimensions due to: not exceeding the permissible strains, not exceeding the permissible displacement and deformation and the minimum mass.

The example of applying variation analysis is creating the reference construction of the gripping bit of the gripper. The initial model is presented in Fig. 3a; on the basis of the results of the variation analysis, as in Fig. 3b and 3c, the optimal reference construction was obtained as presented in Fig. 3d.

Fig. 3

Variation analysis of the construction of gripping bit

In the reference construction, higher strain value (not exceeding the strains limit) was allowed. On that basis, the element mass was reduced by 65%.

## 3 Parametric Construction Record

Parameterization is a specific form of construction record, adapted to the record of series of types of construction (modular series) that are characterized by fixed construction form Π and variable dimension values W. Graphic programs distinguish a few types of parameterization [8]: dynamic, relation, program and graphic parameterization.

Parameterization dynamic is based on manually change the dimension values in a graphics program, using the reference construction, Fig. 4.

Fig. 4

Parameterization dynamic based on the reference construction

Relational parameterization consists of determining mathematical relationships between the dimensions of reference construction and dimensions of the newly created construction These relations are created under the conditions of construction similarities, Fig. 5.

Fig. 5

Parameterization relational on the basis of theory of constructional similarities

The most commonly used parameterization is program parameterization, which uses a programming language: AutoLISP, GRIP, Leverage Phyton in graphics program: AutoCAD Mechanical, NX. The programming language uses a graphical program commands that allowing for integration the selection of design features while recording the construction, Fig. 6.

Fig. 6

Parameterization program with the possibility of calculate the dimensions of the new construction in the calculation program

Graphics parameterization use of the option the graphics program to generate new design, using e.g. from Excel files, and a special software module to create series of types: NX module Part Family. In the Excel file are generated dimensions of new construction based on the reference construction and construction similarities conditions, Fig. 7.

Fig. 7

Graphical parameterization module based on Part Family and Excel

For assemblies, replacing method is used, which is based on changing element of series of types of construction reference for new elements creating a new assembly design, Fig. 8.

Fig. 8

Series of types of construction reference (creating a new assembly design)

## 4 Summary

The main aim of research was to analyze the parameterization process based on similarity theory and reference construction. This is the stage laborious and arduous and therefore it is reasonable to create computer methods. The model of transformation is based on the developed: graphical parameterization, relational parameterization and program parameterization. The analysis results were verified in practice (especially program parameterization and theory of similarity) to construct couplings and components of hydraulic cylinders (pistons, cylinders, piston rod, hydraulic gland). The elements design in form of series of types and modular series. The exponent values were calculated both by theoretical analyze and CAD/CAE simulation.

The test results could be compiled with funds from the DAAD Stipendium 2012.

# Simulations of Air Flow Around the Blades of a Wind Turbine Rotor Using CFD Methods

Tomasz Górnicz1, Tadeusz Lewandowski1  , Romuald Sałacki1 and Wiktor Słomski1

(1)

Wrocław University of Science and Technology, Wyb. Wyspiańskiego 27, 50-370 Wrocław, PL, Poland

Tadeusz Lewandowski (Corresponding author)

Email: tadeusz.lewandowski@pwr.edu.pl

Wiktor Słomski

Email: wiktor.slomski@pwr.edu.pl

Abstract

In this paper were described series of simulations of flow of air around the operating wind turbine blade performed using the methods Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD). Simulations allowed to determine the zero angle at which the turbine should not rotate and projected possible to obtain power of wind turbine in the assumed geometry of the rotor.

While designing a wind turbine, it is crucial to establish what its standard operating parameters should be. This is especially important in terms of nominal power at a particular value of blade's angle of attack, rotor rpm, and speed of wind.

To verify these factors, a research team at the Wrocław University of Technology, performed a number of wind turbine blades' air flow simulations using CFD methods. These analyses were performed on the low power wind turbine (up to 15 kW) designed and developed by the engineering team at Composites Venture & Technology Ltd.

These were done through computer analysis of air flow over the turbine's blades. The results of simulations enabled the team to verify operational parameters of the wind turbine designed by CV&T. They also formed the basis for the design and durability analysis of selected key elements of the mechanical assembly of the designed wind turbine.

Due to periodicity of the analysed phenomena and the repetitive character of the rotor's geometry, the simulation was conducted around a single blade. The diameter of the rotor is 14 m and all tests were conducted on a full scale object.

Turbine operating conditions:

  * wind from 2.5–15 (m/s)

  * rotor revolutions up to 90 (rpm)

Figure 1 shows the reference system, which was used for analysis of the forces affecting the blade and the aerodynamic torque (propulsion) of the wind turbine. It also portrays the blade's placement (rotation in relation to Z-axis).

Fig. 1

The reference system accepted for forces and torques affecting the wind turbine's blade

Air flow calculations were performed with use of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD). The calculation model in use was characterised by the following:

  * Flow of fluids described by Navier-Stokes algorithms,

  * Discretization of algorithms performed with Finite Volume Method (FVM)

  * RANS method was used to solve turbulent air flow,

  * The k-omega SST model was used for turbulence simulation,

  * Boundary layer model was used ("wall function"),

  * The relative reference frame method was used to simulate blade rotation,

  * Periodization of flow was used—periodical boundary conditions.

The accepted shape of the simulation area was cylindrical in shape (Fig. 2) and calculations were performed based on the following boundary conditions:

Fig. 2

A schematic of the computational domain

  * Homogenous averaged field of velocity—entry into the computational domain

  * The Neumann boundary condition—exit of the domain.

  * Viscous wall—blade surface

  * Non-viscous wall—external and internal spherical surface of the domain,

  * Periodical boundary condition—walls directed towards domain radius

To build the discreet model, hexagonal and polyhedral elements were used. A fragment of the discreet model was shown in Fig. 3. Layers of regular elements were placed along the blade's surface (so called "inflation") to picture the phenomena occurring within the boundary layer. The thickness of the first layer of elements placed the closest to blade surface was chosen in such a way as to place the y + parameter (dimensionless factor in relation to the Reynolds number) at about 80. A value like this improves accurate simulation of the boundary layer.

Fig. 3

Discreet choice model. General view of the simplified hub and blade

These are the most substantial simplifications within the geometric model:

  * rounding of the trailing edge

  * modelling of the hub as a non-viscous cylinder.

Both of simplifications had only a marginal effect on the blades aerodynamic properties. In turn, they have significantly improved the quality of the discreet model (element regularity) and enabled acquisition of more accurate simulation data.

In order to minimize the influence of the computational domain size on the analysis, a series of calculations was conducted in regard to domain size. of the domain size have gradually been increased up to the point in which no further changes in aerodynamic properties could be observed. The final size of the domain in relation to the turbines radius [R] is as follows:

  * 4R in front of the turbine surface

  * 8R behind the turbine surface

  * 4R external radius of the domain.

Relationship between grid size and results has also been verified. Simulations have been conducted using normal, fine and super fine grids. No improvement in accuracy of results has been observed with the decrease of the grid sizes (Fig. 4). As a result, all further calculations were conducted with use of the super fine grid. The number of finite elements within the discreet model accounted for about 9.7 mln.

Fig. 4

Examination of relationship between result accuracy and grid size

## 1 Results

  1. (a)

The blades zero angle.

From the perspective of the wind turbine operation adjustment subsystem an important factor was the blades zero angle of attack calculation. the, Blades zero angle of attack is an angle of blades attack at which aerodynamic torque of the rotor equals zero and does not cause the rotor to spin. Calculations were conducted for a wind speed of 8 (m/s) for which the two such blade angles were established:

  * −8.4° (blade postioned at a right angle to the wind),

  * 87.6° (blade position leading-edge first into the wind).

Figures 5, 6 and 7 shows the calculation results of aerodynamic torque and forces affecting the blade in relation to X-axis and Y-axis as a function of the blade's angle of attack at a speed of 8 (m/s) and a stationary rotor.

Fig. 5

Establishing of the blade's zero angles—My = f(alfa)

Fig. 6

Establishing of the blade's zero angles—Fx = f(alfa)

Fig. 7

Establishing of the blade's zero angles—Fy = f(alfa)

The graph of forces on the Y-axis (wind direction) is showing that at an angle of 87 degrees, forces working on a single blade are minimal. Calculated values are shown in Figures 5, 6 and 7.

Part of the analysis focused on the distribution of pressures along the entire surface (windward and leeward). Calculation was conducted for a maximum wind speed of 15 (m/s) and maximum rotor rpm of 90 (rpm). The results will form the basis for an analysis of conditions of stress and durability of the turbine blade. The results of these calculations are shown in Fig. 8.

Fig. 8

Distribution of pressures on the blade's surface, v = 15 (m/s), omega = 90 (rpm)

  1. (b)

The optimal angle of attack for a given operating condition.

Apart of establishing and verifying the operational parameters for the designed wind turbine, an important point considered in the process of all simulations and calculations, was the analysis of the turbine control algorithms This focused particularly on the optimal value of blade angle of attack. For this purpose number of simulations were conducted for different values of wind speed and rotor rpm.

Figure 9 shows sample characteristics established over the course of simulations and calculations. These depict the relationship between aerodynamic torque on a single blade as the function of blade angle of attack at its primary position (defined in its original geometry) and forces on the blade. Optimal values of angle of attack at different turbine operational parameters are shown in Table 1.

Fig. 9

Example relationship between forces and torque working on a rotor blade—similated wind speed of 5 m/s

Table 1

Optimal blade angles of attack

V (m/s) | 2.5 | 5 | 5 | 8 | 8 | 12 | 15

---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---

Omega (rpm) | 30 | 30 | 60 | 60 | 90 | 90 | 90

alfa (deg) | −3 | 2 | −2 | −1 | −2 | −1 | 2

## 2 Summary of Simulation Results

A series of air flows over a working wind turbine blade simulations was conducted. A zero angle of attack was established at which the turbine rotor should not spin. Simulations allowed to establish the forecasted possible wind turbine power considering the given rotor geometry.

At small wind speeds (under 8 m/s) the power generated by the turbine is significantly smaller than 15 (kW). For example:

  * Wind speed 2.5 (m/s), at 30 (rpm), power generated by the turbine is at about 0.7 (kW).

  * Wind speed 5 (m/s), at 60 (rpm), power generated by the turbine is at about 5 (kW).

For wind speeds of above 8 (m/s) the power generated by the turbine is significantly above the projected 15 (kW). Maximum power output generated by the turbine at wind speed of 15 (m/s) and 90 (rpm) is about 93 (kW).

# The Analysis of the Stress Distribution in Contact Pairs Ball-Wire and Wire-Ring in Wire Raceway Slewing Bearing

Dominik Gunia1 and Tadeusz Smolnicki1

(1)

Wroclaw University of Technology, Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Institute of Machine Design and Operation, ul. Lukasiewicza 7/9, 50-371 Wroclaw, Poland

Tadeusz Smolnicki

Email: tadeusz.smolnicki@pwr.edu.pl

Abstract

In the current study the distribution of stresses for four-point contact wire race ball bearing is analyzed. The results for bearings of different geometrical parametric are presented. The study has also estimated the distribution of internal pressure for particular elements.

## 1 Introduction

The wire race slewing bearing is a different kind of slewing bearing, in which a role of raceway executed by a wire. Thank to that, the rings can be made of light metals, like aluminum. Additionally, the wire race slewing bearing are found to be backlash-free and their raceway is found to be easy to change. In such bearing there are two kinds of contact pair: ball-wire and ball-ring. In the ball-wire type of contact pair there are different kinds of phenomenon related to Hertz's theory, whereas the work of the ball-ring type of contact pair should be closely examined before an exploitation, because of the two different elements that may coact.

These types of bearing can be used when there is required particular low weight of bearing. They can be used in aircraft or radars. The wire race slewing bearing can be applied in robotics and medical equipment, because of their backlash-free properties [1]. In the Fig. 1 is represented the example of a cross section of wire race slewing bearing made of carbon fibers [3].

Fig. 1

Section of wire raceway bearing [2]

The four point contact bearing is a kind of bearing in which the rolling elements are responsible for carrying all external components of load. The estimation of the rings deformations, like bearings or any other elements are crucial in predicting how the bearing works. The cross sections of wires in such bearings can have different shapes. However, most often they are used in the circular cross sections. The rolling elements are used as balls or rollers. The use of a finite element method allows for the pair contact analysis and the analysis of the distribution of a pressure for the particular rolling elements. The results of simulations allow for determination of certain characteristics, and allow for making the assumptions in development of alternative four point bearing models [4].

The aim of this study is to investigate the load distribution in particular pairs or pressure and the determination of the most loaded points and characteristics describing stiffness of kinematic pairs, which can be used in development of alternative four-point contact bearing model. Additionally the purpose of this study was also to systematize knowledge about wire race bearing and to begin analyzed behavior of wire race bearing.

## 2 The Characteristics of Wire-Race Bearings

In view of the fact that bearings may differ in terms of a construction, materials used and the type of work, it is necessarily to include all factors that may influence the internal load distribution. The classification of wire-race bearings can depend on:

  1. (a)

The type of rolling elements:

    * balls,

    * rollers,

  2. (b)

The geometry of the bearing:

    * bearing pitch circle diameter D,

    * number of elements z,

  3. (c)

Materials:

    * used in wires: steel, e.g. 54SiCr6,

    * rings: all types of steel, aluminum alloys, bronze, composites,

  4. (d)

Loads:

    * Axial force V,

    * Radial force H,

    * Tilt moment M,

  5. (e)

Shape and a number of wires:

    * Two-point (two wires),

    * Three-point (three wires),

    * Four-point (four wires),

To calculate load bearing capacity the analytical methods can be used, e.g. Ohnrich's method or Matthias's method. However it is worth noting, that they have certain assumptions, like lack of susceptibility of rings, which in case of rings that are made of aluminum alloys it could restrict their use to only estimation of their load capacity and other parameters. In this case, the finite elements method and the possibility of development of the alternative models would be helpful [4, 5].

Hertzian theory can be applied in ball-wire pair. The calculations for this pair does not differ from the methods used in other slewing bearings found in the available literature [4, 6]. However, in wire-ring pair, despite of bigger contact area, contact stress distribution should be checked, especially in case of rings made from aluminum alloys. The risk of crossing the limits of contact stress distribution, could potentially result in plastic deformation of the ring and work of a bearing might be uneven, it may also loosen bearings and bearings may wear off quicker. Therefore, it is important to know the occurring phenomena in such bearings and its mathematic built of model that describe these phenomena.

## 3 Simulation Using Finite Elements Method

In order to simulate FEA phenomena occurring in wire-race bearing, two bearing models with different geometric parameters were built. Furthermore, in order to shorten calculation time for the simulation, cyclic symmetric and mirror symmetric was used, i.e. ¼ of a ball was modelled, and segments of the rings and wires had their parameters equal to half of the scales of bearing. In the contact area, first order HEXA elements were used, whereas in terms of further areas, first order TETRA elements were used. In the Fig. 2 is shown one of the bearing models, arrows represent lack of displacement, and broken arrows symbolize a direction of a kinematic extortion. The parameters of particular bearings are represented in Table 1. A ball and wire was assumed to be made of steel and rings made of aluminum. The ring was firmly fitted to imitate the work of bearing, i.e. radial and axial displacement were blocked. In the model, contact areas have a friction coefficient equal to f = 0.05.

Fig. 2

Bearing model used in simulation with blocked displacement (black arrows) and direction of kinematic extortion (yellow arrows)

Table 1

Geometrical parameters of bearings

Bearing | 1 | 2

---|---|---

Bearing diameter D p (m) | 1 | 2

Ball diameter d k (mm) | 16 | 30

Osculation ratio s | 0.98 | 0.96

The simulation was based on displacement of a reference point inside of a ball with the resultant distance of 0.1 mm in the XY-Plane. Next, Huber-Mises stresses variability was appointed, for a wire and ball in Bielajew point and at the contact edge, whereas for the ring only at the contact edge. Pressure charts were made for contact edge and for the central point in contact area. The distribution of particular deformation of the elements were also checked. The results were presented in function of ball load pw, where the maximum value pw, equals to shifted reference point with the maximum resultant distance. The ball load is defined as:

(1)

where

F

force acting for ball,

d

ball diameter.

An important parameter for wire-race bearings is osculation ratio, simulations were run for two different osculation ratio. Osculation ratio is defined as:

(2)

ball diameter,

r b

wire raceway radius.

An exemplary results of a simulation were presented as plots of Von Mises stresses for bearings number 2 and are shown in the Fig. 3. In the ball-wire pair, higher stress occurred in the wire, and the Bielajew's point lies about 0.3 mm under wire surface. In terms of contact of a wire with a ring, it can be noticed that the stress concentration occurred in the ends of contact. Due to large contact surface, in this pair, stresses are significantly smaller. A maximum value, in the concentration place at the contact edge, equals to σ HM = 111 MPa.

Fig. 3

Von Mises stress plot for bearing 2, for reference point displacement equal 0.03 [mm], [MPa]

It can be concluded that the contact edge of a wire with a ball occurs with the displacement of the reference point in the range of 0.02 and 0.04 mm.

For the displacement in which the contact occurred on the edge of a wire, the percentage distribution was calculated for each of the elements of bearings. The results are presented in the Table 2. The ball was found to be the most easily to deform, on average it accounted for 49% of the bearings deformation. A wire accounted for 39% of deformation, and ring accounted for 12%.

Table 2

Percentage distribution of deformations in bearings (%)

Bearing | Ball | Wire | Ring

---|---|---|---

1 | 51 | 41 | 9

2 | 46 | 37 | 16

The relationship between maximum von Mises stress and ball load is presented in the Fig. 4. Von Mises stress reaches value of σ HM = 2900 (MPa). Higher stress was observed in a wire. This value of stress in Bielajew point was found to correlate with the value found in previous literature [4]. For bearing no. 1 (s = 0.98) ball loads and von Mises stress was higher than in bearing no. 2 This is a result of higher osculation ratio, therefore this bearing can be more loaded [4, 6].

Fig. 4

Comparison of maximum Von Mises stresses in balls and wires, [MPa]

Figure 5 is illustrated the maximum von Mises stress (MPa) for rings. At the edge of the contact area in pair wire-ring in fact, that notch causes stresses are highest. Von Mises stress reaches value of σ HM = 550 MPa. In aluminum alloys it is suggested to decrease this value to maximum 300 MPa, which can be achieved by geometrical correction of this contact [4, 6].

Fig. 5

Comparison of maximum Von Mises stresses in rings, [MPa]

Growth of stresses in rings is linear, whereas in balls and wires is nonlinear. In rings it is an effect of lack of Hertz stress. In balls and wires a nonlinear distribution is a result of Hertz stress and ellipsoidal shape of contact stress. Extractions of Hertz formulas can be found in literature [4, 6].

In case of edge of the contact area of ball-wire, von Misses stress is presented in the Fig. 6. It can be noticed, that the rapid growth of stresses occurs at the time when the ball reaches the edge of a wire. For bearing no. 2 in this case stresses can cross stress in Bielajew point, it is correlated with higher osculation ratio (s = 0.98).

Fig. 6

Comparison of maximum Von Mises stresses on contact edge in balls and wires, [MPa]

According to literature [4] maximum Hertz contact pressure can reach 4200–4600 MPa [4, 6]. An example of the contact pressure plot is presented in the Fig. 7. The maximum contact pressure in the middle of contact in this case is p max = 1760 MPa. This plot is for displacement of the reference for 0.03 mm, which is equivalent to ball load p w = 3.2 MPa. For this value of a ball load occur contact on wire edge. Ellipsoidal shape of contact pressure is visible. The contact pressure plot in case of wire is analogical. There is also a second contact pair present in a wire, this is a wire-ring contact pair, however in this pair contact pressures are significantly lower in comparison to ball-wire contact pair.

Fig. 7

Contact stresses plot for bearing 2, for displacement of reference point 0.03 [mm], [MPa]

The pressure in the middle of a contact is the highest only when ball does not reach a wire edge. For ball contact with a wire edge it can be observed a significant increase of stress and contact pressure. A special correction of wire edge (like curvature or logarithmic correction) should be used to avoid this significant increase [7]. A wire race should be used only in the range of loads which do not lead to contact of a ball with a wire edge, however this situation can happen in unexpected conditions, hence it is necessary to analyze this process.

A distribution of the contact pressures for simulations in the middle of the contact ball-wire is presented in the Fig. 8. For bearing no. 1 contact pressure reaches a value of p max = 4450 MPa, whereas contact pressure for bearing no. 2 is found to be considerably lower (p max = 3400 MPa). Values of contact pressures are in the range of materials strength.

Fig. 8

Comparison of contact pressures p max in the middle of contact pair ball-wire, [MPa]

A distribution of contact pressures at the edge of the contact area of a ball-wire is presented in the Fig. 9. Again, rapid growth of contact pressure is observed when ball reaches the wire edge. Changeability of contact pressures is nonlinear. For bearing no. 2 contact stresses are slightly too high (p max = 5400 MPa), this is presented only for the educational reason.

Fig. 9

Comparison of contact pressure p max on the contact edge in contact pair ball-wire, [MPa]

In the rings contact pressure is shown in the Fig. 10. For contact edge, contact pressures are higher that contact pressures in the middle of a contact (for contact edge p max = 700–750 MPa in the middle of a contact p max = 400 MPa).

Fig. 10

Comparison of contact pressures p max in the middle of contact wire-ring and on the contact edge, [MPa]

## 4 Summary and Conclusions

Four-points contact wire raceway bearings can be analyzed analogically, like normal slewing bearing, however it is important to also analyze contact pair wire-ring, because rings can be made from materials with different properties. In this type of pair, the maximum contact stresses occur at the edge of a contact are (contact stresses are about 50% higher, than those in the middle of a contact), therefore it is essential to provide a geometrical correction for this area.

A next critical point is a contact edge in pair ball-wire, where it is necessary to check this place according to maximum Von Mises stress and contact stress. The geometrical correction for this contact edge is also important, for example, curvature correction, or logarithmic correction could be used. However, well designed wire race bearing should not work on this range of load.

Bearings with higher osculation ratio can reach higher value of von Mises stresses, hence they can be more loaded. However, the effect of contact on wire edge is found to be faster. Additionally, higher von Mises stresses and contact stresses can lead to faster contact wear.

In well-designed wire raceway slewing bearing the most load point is found to be a Bielajew point (the highest Von Mises stress) and the middle of contact in pair ball-wire (the highest contact stress).

Wire raceway bearings can be an alternative for classical slewing bearing in cases where weight is priority. The most loaded parts are: ball and wire, hence ring can be made of materials with lower material strength (like an aluminum).

The next and final advantage of the wire raceway bearings is their changeability properties, hence it can be easily changed of the first sign of a race wear.

# Investigation of Titanium Dioxide Effectiveness of BTX Photocatalytic Oxidation for Automotive Applications Using Advanced Optimisation Algorithms

Aleksander Górniak1  , Anna Janicka1  , Maciej Zawiślak2  and Daniel Michniewicz3

(1)

Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Department of Vehicle Engineering, Wroclaw University of Science and Technology, Braci Gierymskich 164 Street, 51-640 Wroclaw, Poland

(2)

Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Department of Machine Design and Research, Wroclaw University of Science and Technology, Lukasiewicza 7/9 Street, 50-371 Wroclaw, Poland

(3)

Abstract

This paper constitutes the approach of determination the benzene, toluene and xylene (BTX) oxidation properties of titanium dioxide at condition simulating the passenger compartment. Here the oxidation properties of the catalytic agent are considered as its effectiveness. The factors which were under investigation was the temperature, UV light length and the time of pollutant exposition to the catalytic agent. In order to investigate full range of possible solution, the level of variance of all input factors was chosen to be in the maximal possible value which can occur inside a passenger car. Furthermore the experiment was performed according to static, three—dimensional full factorial plan which allowed to developed models of the catalytic agent BTX removal properties. In order to unify the investigation the results were presented as a percentage change of benzene toluene and xylene with respect to the first—reference sample. In consequence the models of titanium dioxide effectiveness are expressed as a second degree polynomial predicting the percentage change of BTX with respect to temperature, UV light length and the time of pollutant exposition. Those models were farther multi objectively optimized in the Pareto sense which allowed to determine optimal condition for the catalytic agent effectiveness within the assumed range of input factors. The complexity of the research and results analyses required usability a variety of computer software starting form constructional software—Autodesk Inventor ending on advanced mathematical environment in which the results were optimised—Matlab optimisation toolbox.

Keywords

BTX photocatalytic oxidationGenetic algorithmsMultiobjective optimizationEffectiveness of TiO2 of BTX oxidationPareto front

## 1 Introduction

One of the most hazardous for human chemical substances are a compounds in which the main, primordial sources are processes of anthropogenic nature. In the case of a passenger compartment of a vehicle the predominant source of hazardous volatile organic compounds (VOC) occurs as a consequence of a co-emission of outer sources (mobile and stationary emitters) as well as inner sources (emission of materials resulting from the vehicle exploitation—for example cigarette smoke). The lowest boiling temperature of the substance (greater volatility), the greater level of hazard of subjecting a human organism to it. Low boiling aromatic hydrocarbon such as benzene, ethylbenzene, toluene and xylene as well as their isomers (BTX) appears to be toxic, mutagenic, and carcinogenic for the cells of respiratory system [6] Therefore, the attempt to remove those compounds in the highest possible extend is fully justified.

Gas purifying properties can be obtained mainly with accordance to three widely used procedures. Firstly the VOCs are adsorbed on the active carbon. This is however rather the form of VOCs displacement than its disposal. The second procedure is bifurcation which is sluggish and its results are rather doubtful. The third is a high temperature oxidation which occurs at temperatures of 200–1000 °C—effective but also expensive. The alternative procedure for VOC removal is a photocatalytic oxidation (PCO) which is more effective, environmental friendly and free from economic issues [10] The most common catalytic agent is titanium dioxide   due to its capability to degrade a wide spectrum of chemical individuals when illuminated with UV light or when in the vicinity of ultraviolet [2, 4, 17, 13] Therefore, it appears that the extend of undesirable, toxic volatile organic compounds removability is dependent upon the UV light length. Furthermore, the reactions can course differently with respect to humidity pressure and temperature. The reaction of BTX oxidation under various condition can in fact cause reduction of one of investigated compounds bud it can also generate another compound as product of the reaction [3, 7].

The literature suggests a vast number of procedures of catalytic agent application or its distribution. For example powdered titanium dioxide can be added to a wall paint for air purification under illumination of UV light from a day light [5, 18, 20]. Another example of the catalytic agent application was deliberated in publication referred under [12]. Here the titanium dioxide was delivered with a brush on a conceal pavement. The thickness of the catalytic agent was 5 μm (40 g facing on m2). The catalytic agent was covered with acryl emulsion. The tests were conducted at constant temperature of 21 °C, resulting in almost 10% reduction of all volatile organic compounds except for toluene (toluene was reduced for 5%).

A procedure of catalytic agent application, interesting in terms of technology is an elastic paper covered or impregnated with photocatalytic material. This procedure however, is not yet fully investigated, but the promising results of a volatile organic compounds reduction justifies further research in this matter [1, 9, 12, 16, 19]. In studies presented in this paper this procedure of catalytic agent application was selected as most convenient, cost efficient and reliable.

## 2 Experiment Set up

Here, the studies are focused in determination of BTX reduction within the passenger compartments, hence the tests are designed in order to simulate the condition existing inside a passenger car. Furthermore, in this studies it is assumed that the most significant source of VOCs is the ventilation. The pollution are aspirated from the exterior of a vehicle mainly in the form of exhaust gases. Taking it into consideration the test station was designed and manufactured in the way enabling simulation of the condition similar to the one existing inside the passenger compartment as well as for convenient data acquisition.

### 2.1 Test Station

During this study it was crucial to evaluate the influence of the time of polluted air exposition to the catalytic agent. For this purpose the air and pollution were flowing within the test station within closed loop. For this reason the test station was equipped with a pipeline and a fan which ensures a closed loop for the flow (see Fig. 1). The air and pollution are entered into the testing loop via two inlets. After delivery of the appropriate amount of air and pollution the valves (indicated with blue colour in Fig. 1) were sealed ensuring the closed flow within the pipe line. The fan ensures constant flow rate.

Fig. 1

The test station

The volume of the closed loop pipeline is 150 L. During this studies it was assumed that the air-pollution mixture shall be composed of 90% of air and 10% of pollution. Therefore, 15 litters of pollutions was introduced to the test station. A reference level is established before each test by performing the experiment without installation of the tested element. The flow rate is set to be 1 m/s of polluted air which is proportional to mass flow rate of 2–3 g/s of the mixture.

For the preparation of an aqueous suspension of titanium dioxide TiO2 were weighed until 4.79 g of titanium oxide (IV) in the form of nanopowder particle size of 21 nm (TEM) with a purity ≥ 99.5% (Aeroxide® P25, Sigma-Aldrich, Germany) in order to maintain the surface charge TiO2 close to 25 g/m2. Powder was added to the test portion of 16 g of water and homogenized to give a consistency of emulsion paint. The suspension was uniformly applied on the surface of the refractory paper by brushing and light rubbing. Refractory paper after application of the aqueous suspension of titanium dioxide was exsiccated in the laboratory dryer. The material was kept at approximately 70 °C for 1 h. Calcination process was performed in a box furnace Nabertherm GmbH N 150 Reheating material for 2 h at 450 °C and kept at that temperature for another 4 h. Then cooled to 25 °C with the inertia of the furnace. From the material, after calcination (clear brittle) matched fittings excised (approximately) to the geometry of the inner walls of the ejector channels and attached to the silicone adhesive, resistant to ultraviolet light (shown in Fig. 2).

Fig. 2

Photocatalytic element with inside the nozzle

### 2.2 Input Factor Selection

The photocatalysis occurs only when the catalytic agent is illuminated with UV light. In consequence the intensity of the light must have influence on the level of compounds reduction by means of photocatalysis. Here, there were three sets of UV lamps selected with accordance to the design of experiment. The range of light length of the available UV lamp is set from 365 to 415 nm. The reason of such a selection is mainly its accessibility and price. Furthermore, light length beyond this range can be hazardous for humans and be the reason of undesirable ozone generation.

The temperature was changed during this study. The range of the temperature is set to resemble the range of temperature within the passenger compartment of a vehicle—17–30 °C. In order to ensure reliable adjustment of the temperature unsusceptible to the weather conditions, whole experiment was performed inside a climatic chamber, which enables control upon the temperature and indirect control upon the humidity.

Samples were collected by YEARS aspirator, model ASP-3 II, flow rate adjusted to 30 dm3/h, the amount of gas collected is 10 dm3. The gas was absorbed on active carbon Anasorb® SKC CSC. Activated carbon is poured into a glass tube of 5 cm3 and later it is emerged in 2 cm3 of carbon disulfide. Volatile organic compounds in the samples was determined by gas chromatography according to the test procedure of the Emission Research Laboratory No. 1/2010 using the gas chromatograph Varian 450—GC with flame ionization detector (FID), and a column Varian VF-WAXms 30 m × 0.25 mm ID DF: 0.25 um. The work was performed at the set temperature of the column 373 K (110 °C), the dispenser 523 K (250 °C) and detectors 423 K (150 °C). YEARS aspirator, model ASP-3 II, flow rate adjusted to 30 dm3/h, the amount of gas collected is 10 dm3, collected samples. The gas was absorbed on active carbon Anasorb® SKC CSC. Activated carbon is poured into a glass tube of 5 cm3 and later it is emerged in 2 cm3 of carbon disulfide. The glass tube is sealed with a stopper. Extraction takes place in a period of 20 min. After every few minutes the contents of the bottle was shaken in order to ensure adequate mixing of the material. Then 5 µl of solution is gathered from above of the carbon layer. Gathered sample is injected into the chromatograph. Compounds designated as "residuals" have been converted to the concentration corresponding to n-pentatonic acid. In other words residuals are the compounds existing within the gas mixtures but was not identified by the chromatograph. The total relative error of the method was estimated at 20% (according to PN—EN ISO 16017-1: 2006).

### 2.3 Design of Experiment

The research conducted during this studies was performed according to carefully selected and designed experiment normalized by norm PN-EN 3534-3. In order to obtain accurate model precisely describing the relationship between the input factors and the result a static, three—dimensional full factorial plan was chosen. This kind of plan assumes that the input factors represent three levels of variation. In consequence a model in the form of second—degree polynomial can be developed. Such a polynomial, describing nonlinear relationships can be farther optimized. Furthermore, due to more detail nature a three—dimensional plans are recommended when linear approximation is inadequate [8, 11, 14, 15]. Here, the volatile organic compounds were be considered separately. Therefore, each compound were described with separate mathematical model, hence the optimization must be performed multi objectively in the Pareto sense. In consequence, the most optimal value of temperature and UV light length and the exposition time will be determined. It should be however emphasized that the mathematical model is valid only in the tested range. Extrapolation beyond the assumed range of the temperature, UV light length, or the exposition time may cause significant errors.

This studies assumes three input factors (i.e. temperature, UV lamps and time of pollutant exposition to the catalytic agent), therefore it is necessary to conduct 27 test types. All input factors are set to be discreet, hence having precise value. This value is set to be a central point of the range of the particular factor [8, 11, 14, 15].

The range of light length of the available UV lamp is set from 365 to 415 nm. The reason of such a selection is mainly its accessibility and price. Furthermore, light length beyond this range can be hazardous for humans and be the reason of undesirable ozone generation.

The temperature was changed during this study. The range of the temperature is set to resemble the range of temperature within the passenger compartment of a vehicle—17–30 °C. In order to ensure reliable adjustment of the temperature unsusceptible to the weather conditions, whole experiment was performed inside a climatic chamber, which enables control upon the temperature and indirect control upon the humidity.

Time of pollutant exposition to the test station varied from 10 to 60 min. Taking into consideration that the source of pollution implemented to the test station was an exhaust gases it was impossible to provide unchanged composition of the gas mixture. Hence the first sample—gathered for first 10 min of the experiments constitutes about the gas composition and initial concentration of all compounds. Therefore this sample was considered as a reference. Subsequent samples (i.e. sample 1, 2, 3) are deliberated with respect to the reference sample. The procedure of sample collection is shown in Fig. 3.

Fig. 3

Procedure of samples collection

The significance of the model was set to be as much accurate as possible in studies related to chemistry. In technological investigation the significance level is usually set to  . However, chemical reaction are subjected to vast number of unpredictable factors, therefore the development of regression model requires lower accuracy. Hence, the significance adjusted for each of tested catalytic agent was   which means that there is 90% of chance that the developed relationships are true [8, 11, 14, 15].

## 3 Results and Discussion

The results of the test performed according to design of experiment) cannot be fully deliberated in terms of statistics. It is because the regression model of benzene reduction properties turned out to be inadequate and unrepeatable. The calculated coefficients of Fisher test and Cochran test showed the most significant deviation from allowed values. The attempt to perform a multi objective optimisation with unpredictable equation of benzene would corrupt the overall results. For this reason, the optimisation was performed only for two objective function (i.e. models of toluene and xylene).

It appeared that the titanium dioxide caused very intensive and hard to predict chemical reaction. Vast amount of unwanted volatile organic compounds was detected during each test. This study however, focuses only on BTX removal properties due to the fact that only these compounds are multi objectively optimised here.

Taking the results of the tests of the catalytic agent illuminated wit UV light length of 415 nm (depicted in Fig. 4) into consideration it appears that the temperature of 30 °C benzene is being generated. The increase of compounds occurs as a consequence of chemical reaction enhanced by the catalytic agent and it existed in previous cases. However, only here a compound raised for over 40%. At this temperature, only benzene is being generated. Considering toluene and xylene the graduate reduction in time can be noticed. When the test was carried out at the temperature of 23.5 °C the results showed surprisingly high effectiveness of catalytic agent. Here, especially benzene is susceptible to the photocatalysis. The tests carried out at temperature of 17 °C resulted in the highest percentage effectiveness of the catalytic agent at the end of the tests (sample 3). It appeared that the firs sample shewed the lowest BTX reduction and the subsequent sample represent similar gas purification properties.

Fig. 4

BTX oxidation by means of titanium dioxide

When the catalytic agent is illuminated with 390 nm of UV light length, at the temperature of 30 °C the percentage of BTX reduction is approximately the same for first two samples. The second repetition however, indicates that the highest reduction of volatile organic compounds exists on the beginning and in the end of the process. The intermediate time provokes decrease in BTX reduction. Opposed tendency can be observed in the results gathered during the tests at 23.5 °C. Here, the best reduction increases with time for benzene and toluene. Taking into consideration the results of the tests performed at temperature of 17 °C it appears that first two samples indicates similar BTX removal capabilities while the last sample shows the highest effectiveness for compounds reduction.

As in any other case illuminating the catalytic agent with UV light length of 365 nm results in a large variability preventing from drawing accurate conclusion. It appears that the shortest light length provokes most significant and entirely unpredictable reactions. This case however, comparing with the other, is the source of the greatest distortion of the results and might be the reason of inadequate equation of regression.

The equation of regression obtained basing on the designed experiment are presented as Eqs. 1–3. Equation of regression for benzene reduction (Eq. 1) however, has been proven to be inadequate (Fisher test), and according to Cochran criterion the measurements cannot be consider as reliable. Therefore, this equation was excluded from further deliberation. The equation of regression for toluene (Eq. 2) was adequate, however the repeatability of tests can be questioned. Despite these not reliable results, this model was considered as possible and was subjected to the multi objective optimisation. The equation of regression for xylene removability was proven to be adequate and reliable according to Fisher test and Cochran criterion respectively.

### 3.1 An Approach to Optimisation of the Input Factors

In order to find the optimal condition for the catalytic agent to purify the pollution the Pareto multi objective optimisation was programmed. Thus, the result of optimisation will be the set of temperature, UV light length and time of exposure, which provokes the highest catalytic agent effectiveness. Taking into consideration that the models which has been developed basing on the test results constitutes the percentage availability to reduce undesirable compounds the optimisation must consists on multi objective maximisation. All optimisation was performed in Matlab environment using genetic algorithms. In general, genetic algorithms search for possible solution of the objective function. The solution of a particular computation is called an individual. The algorithm, in every iteration creates a population consisting on number of individuals. Then the individuals are confronted in order to select the best one (i.e. the result closest to the objective function) which then is transfer to the next generation. The iteration is repeated until a stop criterion is met. In this studies the algorithm searches a 3D space combined of input factors—temperature, time of exposure, and UV light length. The range of searching (called the environment) is enclosed by maximal and minimal values of those impact factors. Taking into consideration that the genetic algorithms are a global optimisation tool the optimisation may result in determination of set of local optima.

Here, the population was set to 50 of individuals, which were inherited by means of tournament method of the selection. Individuals were mutated according to adaptive feasible method, and the Pareto front population was set for 0.7. Stopping criteria was reaching 500 generation or obtaining average change in the spread of Pareto solutions less than options.

Taking into consideration that the default Pareto optimisation in Matlab consists on minimalizing the objective function it was necessary to alter the objective function. It was done by dividing one by the objective function (Eqs. 4a, 5a, and 6a). Minimising such a functions will result in maximisation of an overall result.

(4a)

Matlab calculates Pareto front by minimising the assumed objective functions finding parameters associated with global minimum. An example of Pareto front obtained during the optimisation process is shown in Fig. 6. Here, two objectives are confronted with each other. Objective 1 represents minimisation of toluene function and Objective 2 represents xylene function. Therefore, this chart represents the change of toluene and xylene with respect to each other. As it was already mentioned the equation for benzene was excluded from this deliberation due to its inadequacy.

The Pareto front for the maximization of the toluene and xylene percentage removal is shown in Fig. 6. Here the chart indicates at least two local maxima of the functions distant from each other. It appears that there is a significant gap between the individuals presented in the Pareto front. This is farther proven by the score histogram depicted in Fig. 7. Taking into consideration multi objective maximization it might be concluded that for titanium dioxide two sets of UV lamps changeable with respect to the temperature should be implemented.

Here the values of input parameters, which corresponds to the highs effectiveness of volatile organic compounds reduction, are shown in Table 1. Therefore, particular caution should be given when analysing the optimisation results of titanium dioxide.

## 4 Conclusion

The tests performed with accordance to the carefully planned and designed experiment allowed to develop models, which after multi objective optimization allowed to determine optimal values of temperature, UV light length and time of exposure to the catalytic agent. Titanium dioxide however, is proven to enhance reaction with significant variability, thus the models developed for benzene was proven to be untrustfull on the level of significance of  . The results of xylene and toluene are considered as possible.

The experiments, which consisted on two repetition of the tests. The developed mathematical models includes therefore the variation of those two repetition. Furthermore, the algorithm was not standardized, therefore it was not able to select a particular UV lamp but only an optimal UV light length. The multi objective optimization consisted on confronting objective function and evaluating the best solution. Hence the result of optimization constitutes an optimal condition for the particular catalytic agent to remove BTX.

Taking the results of measurements into consideration, it appears that xylene in most cases is the most vulnerable to the catalytic agent purifying properties. Benzene showed opposite tendency. Its removability is in most cases the lowest amount the other compounds.

# Analysis of Construction and Internal Load of the Powertrain of the Prototypical Four-Wheeled Mobile Platform

Anna Jaskot1  , Bogdan Posiadała1  and Szczepan Śpiewak1

(1)

Institute of Mechanics and Machine Design Foundations, Czestochowa University of Technology, Dąbrowskiego 73, 42-201 Częstochowa, Poland

Anna Jaskot (Corresponding author)

Email: jaskot@imipkm.pcz.pl

Bogdan Posiadała

Email: bogdan.p@imipkm.pcz.pl

Szczepan Śpiewak

Email: spiewak@imipkm.pcz.pl

Abstract

The designed solution of the powertrain of four-wheeled mobile platform have been developed. Identification of the internal loads has been carried out by using the finite element method. The two analyses based on the internal load of these elements have been performed. The first analysis gave an information about the reduced stress of the driver and a sleeve for the powertrain model, loaded by torque and forces of gravity. The second analysis was performed only for the system loaded by the forces of gravity. The results are presented on the graphs.

## 1 Introduction

Development of techniques of both remote and autonomous steering of electric drives resulted in creation of innovative solutions in constructions of machines used to handling systems. The example of handling devices includes production cells is a wheeled mobile platform. At the Institute of Mechanics and Machine Design Foundations the research applied to the mathematical description of kinematics and dynamics phenomena of machines and devices for various purposes is being carried out for many years. The studies aiming to adapt proven research methods in order to analysis of problems connected with wheel's motion of the mobile platforms have been undertaken for few recent years. At present, the design work on the prototypical construction solutions of the four-wheeled mobile platform are underway. Thorough research of dynamical interactions and their impact on the smooth motion is the base to determine the central control settings of drive units of the drive transmission system and of the steering system. So far the kinematics and dynamics of the prototyped model of mobile platform have been described. Determining the motion's parameters with studies about the behavior of platform during steady [5] and unsteady motion is a subject of other studies.

This work concerns the strength analysis of the main elements included in the drive transmission system.

## 2 Technical Characteristic of the Research Object

The subject of research is an author's developed construction solution of the wheeled transporter, in which the chassis system is pictorially represented in Fig. 1.

Fig. 1

Illustration of construction of chassis of the designed wheeled mobile platform

Before developing the system to meet the industrial functions, the verification of determined models of machine motion must be carried out. These models will provide the user a safe realization of identified tasks.

The basic concept of design solution of presented system, which currently is only the object of the laboratory studies, involves the construction of modular design. Creating configurations of selected positioning of the platform wheels is possible by the using the drive member with electric drive. The described version of the unaided chassis of the research platform is developed on the basis of the introduced assumptions and constructed with the rigid frame (1) on the sides of which the main hitches (2) of the steering spindle (4) (also named as stub axle) are attached in a clamping way.

Different configurations of the hitches allow to changes the distance the axis of the drive wheels (3) along the longer side of the frame. Each wheel has an independent drive system constituting the coupling of the electric motor (5) with a planetary gear in coaxial system (5). The symmetry axis of the steering spindle (4) passes through the center of gravity of the motor assembly, the planetary gear, the road wheel and a driver (6). Through the driver the torque is transmitted from the gear to the road wheel. In order to provide a small rotational motion resistance, for the road wheels and drivers the bearing system has been provided.

The torsion system of the platform, according to the initial assumption, is dependent in pairs, and is realized through an electric motor conjugated to the worm gear (7), a rod system (9) and a rack and pinion gearing (8). In addition, it is possible to embed an independent stub axle drives on the hitches (2). The body chassis is mounted to the chassis frame. Due to the defined scope of application of the platform it is assumed that the maximum angle of elevation which the vehicle can effectively overcome is 5°. It can be ensured by the brushless motors type BG42 produced by Dunkermotoren [3], with a power rating amounts to 40 (W) providing nominal (continuous) torque of 0.105 (N m) at nominal rotational velocity 3650 (r/min). Nominal motor parameters assure its highest efficiency with amounts of 72%. Coupling of engine with planetary gear with a gear ratio of 100 and efficiency of gear of 0.73% should allow the transport of materials with a weight per single drive unit of 170 kg at zero slope of the road, and 80 kg at a maximum angle of elevation.

## 3 Construction and Rule Action of the Powertrain of Wheels

For the purpose of realization, the design requirements included in the previous section the constructional solution of the drive transmission system, which pictorially is presented in Fig. 2, have been developed. The assembly is rotationally coupled to the frame of the platform through a steering spindle (1). The steering spindle is welded to the fork (3) constituting the main load-carrying element of the assembly. A drive motor (8), coupled axially to the planetary gear (9), is embedded in the main sleeve (5) by means of screws (15). The main sleeve (5) is used to relieve the bending stresses of the stator housing of the electric motor and thus of the gear. The main sleeve (5) is embedded in the stub axle centering hole (3) and bolted (14). The torque is transmitted from the output shaft of the gear (9) via a groove (11) on the sleeve of the driver (4). The sleeve of the driver is embedded through the roller radial bearing (17) in support of fork (2).

Fig. 2

Powertrain of road wheel of the platform

The support of fork is attached to the fork by means of bolts (12). The driver (4) is attached to the road wheel rim (6) via a loosely embedded bolts (13) in the hole of the driver. The free rotational motion of the drive wheel with both the coupling and uncoupling of the driver by screws (13) is realized by the needle roller bearing (16). The bearing is further secured by clamp (10). On the rim is embedded wear layer of the tread (7). In the presented system the driver (4) fulfills two functions simultaneously. It provides torque transfer and through connection with the support of fork (2) is a supporting element for the sleeve (5). Therefore, its internal load will depend on the angular position in relation to the force vector of gravity. So, it is loaded simultaneously with torque and the forces of gravity. The individual parts of the driver structure will carry both bending and torsional stresses.

Usage of bearing (16) should ensure the freeing the sleeve (5) from torsional stresses. From mechanical point of view, the sleeve (5) will be a bilaterally supported beam loaded by the bending moment. Such a system can be classified as a statically indeterminable system. When the drive will disconnected, e.g. when the bolts (13) will be removed, the sleeve (5) will be a beam unilaterally fixed. The spindle (3) can be modeled as a spatial frame.

## 4 Strength Analysis of Powertrain of Drive Wheels

Considering the designed system by taking into account the selection of materials for individual support elements, there is a need to perform an identification of internal loads occurring in the main components of the assembly.

More precise determination of stresses, which cannot exceed the allowable stress values in the designed system required using the numerical methods. The calculation model of the assembly of cooperating components, presented in Fig. 2, should take into account the susceptibility of the carrier elements as well as the conditions of mutual contact surfaces. Of particular importance may be higher susceptibility of the wheel tread in relation to susceptibility of the ground (S) and the susceptibility of the other constructional components of the system.

Therefore, in order to identify the internal loads, the finite element method was used. FEM model and calculations were performed by using the ADINA system. In order to reduce the sizes of the task, thereby shortening the calculation time, the discretization structure of the main sleeve (5), the driver (4) road wheel rim (6) and the tread (7), which is in contact with the road, were the main aspect of the task. Mapping the FE mesh model of the powertrain shown in Fig. 2 is presented in Fig. 3. In order to ensure the possibility of defining different strength parameters for materials, of which the selected components of the assembly will be performed, the FE model are grouped. The particular groups denoted by numbers is described in Fig. 3.

Fig. 3

The FE mesh model of the powertrain of the platform's drive wheel

The different FE groups (Fig. 3) have been mapping the geometric structure of the fork (1), of the tread (2), of the driver (3), of the wheel rim (4), of the clamp (5), of the main sleeve (6), of the support of fork (7), of the steering spindle (8) and, of the ground (9), which was introduced for the modeling purpose. All model's objects have been discretized by eight-nodal FE type of 3D-Solid [1]. Between the clamping surfaces, nascent in the real objects in a result of bolt tension forces the "glue" type, boundary conditions [1] have been applied. This type of conditions ensure immutability in position of the relative position of nodes of different groups of FE during the load simulation.

A prerequisite to correctly configure displacements "glue" type, is that set of nodes of particular groups of FE will form a separate common flat surface in the plane of contact of the modeled objects. Rolling bearings in the model was replaced by the contact groups separated for couples of FE groups 3–7 and 4–6. Detailed terms of rolling friction in rolling bearings are replaced with the terms of the sliding friction coefficient of friction equals to 0.0015 [7]. Similar conditions defined of contact between groups 2–9 by defining the value of the coefficient of sliding friction equal to 0.6. In this case it allowed to simultaneous mapping of rolling and sliding friction taking into account the deformability (flexibility) of the material of the tread and the ground. It was assumed that the tread is made of Vulkollan [2] and the ground will be close to the material properties of the steel. In the material models of each group of FE were assumed the linear relations between stress and deformation by introducing the modulus and Poisson's ratio to calculation in accordance with the data of Table 1.

Table 1

Parameters of material models of particular FE groups of powertrain model of the platform's wheel drive

No group of FE model according to Fig. 3 | Name of material | The longitudinal elastic modulus MPa [4, 5] | Poisson ratio [4, 5]

---|---|---|---

1 | Aluminium PA6 | 72,500 | 0.33

2 | Vulkollan | 630 | 0.40

3 | Mild steel | 200,000 | 0.35

4 | Mild steel | 200,000 | 0.35

5 | Mild steel | 200,000 | 0.35

6 | Aluminium PA6 | 72,500 | 0.33

7 | Aluminium PA6 | 72,500 | 0.33

8 | Aluminium PA6 | 72,500 | 0.33

9 | Mild steel | 200,000 | 0.35

Interaction between the output shaft of the epicyclic gearing and the driver was determined by receiving degrees of freedom (DOF) for the two components of the displacement direction of the nodes describing the sleeve hole of the driver (as illustrated in the side view of the model—Fig. 3).

Occurring the forces of gravity in the model was implemented by putting the concentrated force Q to the corner node of the ninth group. In order to eliminate the peculiarities, the displacement conditions of node were bounded with boundary conditions of displacements of nodes (on the bottom and side walls of the cuboidal block), which represented the base of infinite length, width and height.

The value of statically acting force Q was equal 1668 (N). The torque defined by the peripheral action of the concentrated forces (which are components of the resultant force F) were applied to the nodes with distance about half of the diameter of the tread. The value of the resultant force F is determined based on the torque of the output shaft of gear, and taking into account its efficiency. Model calculations were made due to the complexity of the loads condition of the main sleeve and the driver. It was stated that these elements are particularly vulnerable to destruction. Two analyses of internal load of these elements have been performed. The first analysis gave an information about the reduced stress of the driver and of the sleeve for the powertrain model loaded by the torque and by the forces of gravity. Contours of the reduced stresses of the driver and the sleeve are presented in Figs. 4 and 5.

Fig. 4

Contours of the reduced stresses of the driver determined during the first analysis

Fig. 5

Contours of the reduced stresses of the sleeve determined during the first analysis

The second analysis was performed for the servo system in which the driver isn't coupled with the rim. In the model the boundary conditions, of the glue type for nodes of groups 3–4, were deactivated.

The system was loaded with only the forces of gravity. The reduced stress distribution for the sleeve shown in Fig. 6.

Fig. 6

Contours of the reduced stresses of the sleeve determined during the second analysis

## 5 Summary and Conclusions

On the basis of the calculation performed during the first analysis, it was found that the maximum reduced stresses in both the driver and the sleeve does not exceed the yield point, for which the sleeve material is 145 MPa and driver material is 235 MPa. The obtained values of safety coefficients are 1.96 for the driver and 4.8 for the sleeve. The second analysis showed nearly twice higher maximum value of the reduced stress of the sleeve. Since in this case the sleeve operates in a jib way, the location of the maximum stresses is different than in the first loading case. It is due to the fact that the driver function is working as a rotational support and is taking over some of the forces of gravity.

It can be stated that the designed system should meet the strength requirements for the accepted parameters of the drive unit. Identified stresses do not reach the limits of fatigue. The model can also be used to analyses the rolling resistance [6] of a wheel—pavement pair with different material parameters. The results of such analyses in correlation with the dynamic model of the platform will include the subject of further publications.

# CFD Model of an External Gear Pump

Paulina Jędraszczyk1 and Wiesław Fiebig1

(1)

Wrocław University of Science and Technology, Wrocław, Poland

Wiesław Fiebig

Email: wieslaw.fiebig@pwr.edu.pl

Abstract

The paper presents a CFD model of an external gear pump. To investigate the fluid flow phenomena that occur in external gear pumps, one of the commercial CFD software packages was selected. The immersed solid method was used to simulate the flows induced by the rotation of gears. The article presents results of simulation studies carried out for various operating parameters of a chosen external gear pump. Prepared 2D CFD model was used to consider the influence of rotational speed and the pressure in the outlet channel on the cavitation intensity. Furthermore, the 3D simulation model was prepared to verify the pressure relief groves impact on the pressure distribution and velocity contours in the area of gears engagement, as well as mass flow rate and pressure pulsation on the outlet.

## 1 Introduction

Gear pumps belong to a group of positive displacement pumps. Their cost-effectiveness, simple construction and compactness makes them commonly used in both stationary and mobile hydraulic drives.

The volumetric efficiency of this pumps decrease because of fluid flow occurring in the axial gaps between sides of the gears and bearings surfaces as well as in radial gaps existing between the tooth heads and the casing [1–7]. Taking into account fluid volume changes in spaces between gears teeth, especially in the meshing zone, the cavitation phenomena can take place [4, 7].

The design of gear pumps and motors is focused on more efficient units which is possible with advanced numerical simulation techniques. To investigate all of mentioned processes CFD model was prepared, which enables to study fluid flow phenomena during the pumps operation.

## 2 External Gear Pump 2D CFD Model

The physical model chosen for the analysis is an external gear pump manufactured by Parker Hannifin Corporation. The PGP620 unit is made up of the three main elements: driving gear (active), driven gear (passive), housing.

Investigated pump operates at speeds from 500 to 3500 rpm and continuous pressures of up to 275 bar. Figure 1 presents the geometrical model of the pump created using CATIA V5 software.

Fig. 1

3D geometry model of an external gear pump created via CATIA V5

### 2.1 CFD Model

Based on three-dimensional model geometry of the gear pump simplified two-dimensional model was created. Then it was discretized using hexahedral mesh with the thickness of one element. The mesh size was chosen to be sufficiently large to speed up calculations and small enough to visualize fluid flow phenomena that occur in the radial gap as well as in meshing zone. For simulation the Immersed Solid Method was used, which is an option of ANSYS CFX program that allows simulation rigid motion of solid objects through fluid regions. Importantly, it avoids any mesh deformation or remeshing.

Figure 2 shows two-dimensional model of the gear pump with selected domains and locations of boundary conditions. In order to obtain results of reasonable accuracy the simulation parameters were set according to the Table 1.

Fig. 2

Simplified 2D model of a PGP620 pump

Table 1

Domains

---

Fluid | Stationary

Inlet | Stationary

Outlet | Stationary

Gears | Rotation

Boundary conditions

Inlet | Pressure inlet

Outlet | Pressure outlet

Housing | Wall

Analysis

Hydraulic oil used as material for fluid domain has following properties:

  * Density—950 kg/m3

  * Kinematic viscosity—37 mm2/s.

### 2.2 Comparison of Experimental and Simulation Results

Results from simulation have been compared with experimental studies presented in [6] for defined positions of gears and equal operating parameters of the pump (rotational speed—500 rpm and discharge pressure—0.55 MPa).

Figure 3 shows velocity vectors plot from CFD simulation results and photo from high speed camera taken during the visualization investigations of the gear pump [6]. In both cases strong disturbances in form of characteristic turbulence of the flow are visible. In this area, except of change of the flow direction, fluid velocity increase. At the same time the pressure in the turbulence zone decrease what is visible on the pressure distribution plot in Fig. 3a.

Fig. 3

Comparison of a simulation, b visualization results

The solution obtained using CFD is in the agreement with results from experimental investigations. Therefore the CFD model can be used for further analysis of fluid flow phenomena in gear pumps.

## 3 Operating Parameters and Their Influence on the Flow

The fluid flow analysis was performed for different operating parameters of the pump such as gears rotational speed and discharge pressure while maintaining the same value of radial gap. All of the cases and sets of parameters considered during research are shown in Table 2. For each set of parameters numerical simulation was performed and then the pressure distribution and velocity vectors in the area of gears engagement were plotted. This enables the analysis of fluid flow processes that appear in this region as well as investigating the intensity of cavitation phenomenon.

---|---|---
